articles.title: The Hardware Hacking Gatekeepers Want You To Think You Need a Degree
articles.description: Spoiler: You don't. You need $30 and a willingness to let the magic smoke out.  I asked a "hardware...
articles.body_html:
Spoiler: You don't. You need $30 and a willingness to let the magic smoke out.

I asked a "hardware hacking expert" on Twitter what I should buy to get started.

He sent me an affiliate link to a $499 course. The course had a $200 toolkit. The toolkit required a $150 oscilloscope add-on.

For $849, I could finally learn how to blink an LED.

That's not education. That's a funnel. And it's working.

If you've ever Googled "how to start hardware hacking" and ended up in a rabbit hole of oscilloscope reviews, JTAG pinout diagrams from 2007, and some guy in a lab coat telling you that you need to understand signal integrity before you touch a board — congratulations. You've met the Gatekeepers.

Their business model depends on you believing that hardware hacking is hard, expensive, and credentialed. It's not. It's just messy.

The Gatekeeping Playbook

Here's how the funnel works:

Step 1: Invent a prerequisite. "You can't hack hardware until you understand electrical engineering fundamentals."

Oh really? You need to understand MOSFET physics to dump firmware off a cheap smart plug? Tell that to every 14-year-old in Shenzhen who is already doing it.

Step 2: Weaponize the "What should I buy first?" question.

This is the most profitable question in all of hardware. Every beginner asks it, because they are terrified of buying the wrong thing. So the Gatekeepers turn anxiety into a shopping list.

You need:

  • A $400 oscilloscope (minimum)
  • A $150 soldering station (Hakko or nothing)
  • A Bus Pirate, a Shikra, a GreatFET, a ChipWhisperer, and a partridge in a pear tree
  • A degree, or at least their $500 course that is basically a degree

What happens? You spend $1,200, get overwhelmed, never open the boxes, and conclude that "hardware is too hard for me."

Mission accomplished. The priesthood remains small. Their course completion rate stays low enough that they never have to provide support.

Step 3: Confuse complexity with depth.

They'll show you a glitching attack on a secure enclave that took a team of PhDs six months, and imply that that's what hardware hacking is.

That's like showing someone a Formula 1 engine rebuild and saying "you can't learn to drive until you can do this."

Real hardware hacking for 99% of us is much dumber, much more fun, and much more useful: Can I talk to this chip? Can I dump this firmware? Can I make this device do something the manufacturer didn't want it to do?

You don't need a degree for that. You need permission to break things.

The $30 Heresy

Here's the actual starter kit that every gatekeeper hates because it makes their course irrelevant:

1. A $20 ESP32 Dev Board
Not an Arduino. An ESP32. It has WiFi, Bluetooth, more pins than you'll know what to do with, and a community that has already reverse engineered everything. It's insecure by design, which makes it perfect to learn on. You can flash it, brick it, re-flash it, sniff its traffic, and it costs less than lunch. Buy two, because you WILL brick one. That's the point.

2. A $10 Logic Analyzer (the cheap Chinese Saleae clone)
The little black 8-channel USB thing on and AliExpress that looks like a knockoff. It is a knockoff. It also works perfectly.

The Gatekeepers will tell you you need an oscilloscope. You don't. Not yet. An oscilloscope shows you analog reality — voltage wiggles. A logic analyzer shows you digital truth — is this pin talking 1s and 0s, and what is it saying? 90% of beginner hardware hacking is just eavesdropping on two chips gossiping via UART, SPI, or I2C. This $10 dongle plus free PulseView software lets you do that on day one.

3. Permission to Break Things (Free)

This is the most expensive item because no one wants to give it to you.

Every tutorial teaches you how to build. Almost none teach you how to break. But breaking is the skill.

Buy a $5 smart plug from Walmart. Open it. Find the UART pads (they're almost always there, unlabelled, laughing at you). Solder some janky wires to them. Connect your $10 analyzer. Get garbage data. Swap TX and RX. Get readable boot logs. Feel like a god.

That feeling is the whole game. No course can sell it to you.

What They Don't Tell You About Learning

The industry education funnel is built on a lie: that you learn linearly. First theory, then tools, then practice.

Real hackers learn backwards. We call it "just-in-time learning."

You don't learn what UART is by reading a textbook chapter on serial protocols. You learn it because you have a board in front of you that is spewing garbage at 115200 baud and you NEED to know why it's garbage.

You don't learn to solder by practicing on a practice board. You learn to solder because your wire keeps falling off that tiny pad and you are angry.

Desperation is a better teacher than any curriculum. The $30 kit creates desperation. The $849 kit creates procrastination.

Think about software hacking. No one tells you "you must master C, assembly, operating system theory, and networking before you can run nmap." They tell you to install Kali and break stuff. We accept that in software because the tools are free.

In hardware, the tools cost money, so people can gatekeep with them.

The 3 Projects That Actually Teach You To Think

If you bought the $30 kit, do this, in this order. Don't watch 40 hours of video first.

Project 1: The Sniff.
Take any IoT device you own — old router, smart bulb, cheap IP camera from Amazon. Open it. Identify the chips. Google the chip numbers + "datasheet". Find the TX/RX/GND pins. Hook up your logic analyzer. Capture the boot log. You just did what 80% of "IoT security consultants" charge $300/hour to do.

Project 2: The Dump.
Get that ESP32. Flash it with some open-source firmware like Tasmota. Then dump the firmware back off it using esptool. Then open the dump in a hex editor and find the WiFi password you hardcoded. Congratulations, you now understand why firmware extraction is a threat model. No oscilloscope needed.

Project 3: The Lie.
Take that smart plug. Find its cloud endpoint in the boot log or the firmware. Block it at your router. Watch the device freak out. Use your ESP32 to spoof a fake server that tells the plug "yeah, you're connected to the cloud, totally." You just did an evil twin / MITM attack on hardware.

Each project will force you to learn exactly three things you didn't know before. That's sustainable. That's how you actually get good.

The gatekeeper path? Project 1 is "Learn Ohm's Law for 6 weeks."

Which one do you think keeps people in the field?

Why They Do It

I'm not saying all educators are scammers. Some are amazing. But the incentive structure is broken.

You can't sell a $19 guide that says "buy cheap stuff and break it" for $500. You need to manufacture complexity to justify the price.

You need to make it sound like you need THEM. Like hardware is a sacred temple and they are the priest who will grant you entry, for a fee.

The truth is much more punk rock: The manufacturers are leaving debug interfaces wide open. The chips have default passwords. The firmware is often not even encrypted. The hardware industry itself has done zero opsec, and it's begging to be poked at with a cheap tool.

You don't need their blessing. You need a screwdriver.

The best hardware hackers I know don't have EE degrees. They have a drawer full of dead boards, burnt fingers, and a habit of saying "what happens if I short this pin?"

That's not a credential. That's a mindset. And you can't buy it.

You can, however, get a head start without the $500 tax.

Look, I got tired of watching smart people get scared off by shopping lists designed to sell courses. So I wrote the anti-course.

It's not a video series. It's not 40 hours. It's a field manual: the exact $30 cart, where to solder without destroying the pads, the 5 dumpster-dived devices to practice on, and the PulseView settings that actually decode UART the first time instead of the fifth.

If you want the no-bullshit, no-gatekeeping version I wish someone had handed me on day one, it's here:

The $19 'Permission to Break Things' - My Complete Beginner Hardware Hacking Field Kit on Gumroad — includes the parts list, wiring diagrams, and the first 5 projects that make you dangerous.

Or don't buy it. Honestly, just buy the ESP32 and the logic analyzer and start breaking stuff. That's the real guide anyway.

The gatekeepers will hate you for it.

articles.title: Avoid These 4 Claude Code Context Antipatterns
articles.description: Four ways to quietly pollute your Claude Code context, and how to fix each one with /clear, /rewind, subagents, and a lean CLAUDE.md.
articles.body_html:
The 4 Context Antipatterns

Claude Code is powerful. However, it is easy to accidentally mess up your own session if you're not careful with context. Anthropic’s Claude Code docs list five common failure patterns. I'm going to go over four of them.

Antipattern 1: The Overstuffed Fridge

You want to build a button. You start Claude Code. Halfway through, you ask Claude something random: "Hey, can you explain OAuth?" Claude answers. You go back to building a button. That's cool, but now your context contains both.

Claude's context is like a fridge. It has finite space. When you mix unrelated stuff in, everything gets harder to find. Quality degrades. Claude re-reads all that OAuth stuff every time you ask about the button. It is not giving 100% attention to the button anymore.

Instead, /clear (aliases: /new or /reset) between unrelated tasks. Doing so wipes context and starts you fresh. Your next task gets Claude's full attention.

If your mind wanders like mine, keep a separate Claude session just for those questions.

You can use /btw for a quick side question. The answer never enters your conversation, so your context stays clean.

A fresh context with a focused prompt is better than a cluttered one.

Antipattern 2: The Correction Rabbit Hole

Claude writes code. The result doesn't look right. You correct it: "Make the button smaller." Good, but something is still off. "Make the edges rounder." Again. Again. By the tenth correction, your context is full of attempts. Claude drowns in noise. Each correction doesn't erase the last one. It adds to the pile. "Instead, can you..." adds a new line. Each line is context spent.

Instead, after two failed attempts, /clear and restart with a better prompt. You want Claude to stay sharp. Don't clutter context with corrections. Make every token count.

Don’t do the tenth “no, try this.” Start fresh instead. This time, be precise: “In SubmitButton.tsx, reduce the button height from 48px to 40px, reduce the horizontal padding from 24px to 16px. Shift it 10px left by changing margin-left from 24px to 14px. Make the corners fully rounded with border-radius: 9999px. Keep the font size.” Include what you learned. A clean slate with a better prompt is better than noisy, endless corrections.

Catch mistakes early. Press Esc to stop Claude mid-action. If a turn already went wrong, press Esc Esc (or /rewind) and roll back to before it. A rewind removes the bad attempt instead of piling a correction on top.

Antipattern 3: The Marco Polo Session

You ask Claude: "Investigate why user authentication is slow." Claude reads files. More files. Then more files. Giant log files! Suddenly your context is thousands of lines deep. Claude explores things that probably don't matter.

Claude is like Marco Polo. It likes to explore, and when it does, it explores wide. Claude can read a lot of files faster than a human, but it also fills context with noise faster than I can fill my shopping cart on Black Friday with stuff I don't need. By the time you get an answer, your context is filled up with expedition notes.

Scope the investigation. Or hand it off. Instead of "Investigate why user authentication is slow," say: "Look only at the session lookup in src/auth/. Find slow database queries." Claude now has boundaries and it explores narrow.

Maybe you don't know the boundaries. If you want it to search far and wide, use a subagent. Ask: “Use a subagent to investigate why the login endpoint is slow. Read the relevant files and report back a summary.” The subagent explores in its own context. You get a clean summary. All the file-reading stays in the agent's context, not in your main conversation.

To spawn an investigation in the background while you work on the main task, use /subtask (requires Claude Code v2.1.212 or later). /subtask investigate why user authentication is slow forks a subagent that inherits your current conversation and reports back when it’s done. A subagent is like delegating to an assistant. "Go figure this out. Come back with a summary." The assistant can explore far and wide and that context stays with it. It never enters the main conversation. What comes back is just the brief result.

Antipattern 4: The Overstocked Staples

If Claude's context is your fridge, CLAUDE.md is your staples: milk, eggs, butter (almost every fridge has them, and almost every meal starts from them). Claude loads CLAUDE.md into every session, so whatever you put there takes up space in every conversation.

The problem starts when you have too many “staple” items. Do you really need 2% milk, 1% milk, and whole milk? Maybe just pick one. Do you need four half-empty bottles of different hot sauces instead of one? Do you need a dozen regular-sized eggs and a dozen large cage-free eggs?

Pretty soon you can't find your hot sauce and your milk spoils. A bloated CLAUDE.md works similarly. Important rules get lost in the noise. Claude starts ignoring half of them. Like that milk, old rules go stale. Anthropic suggests keeping each CLAUDE.md under 200 lines. For each line, ask: “Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?” If Claude does fine without it, cut it.

Keep in mind that splitting CLAUDE.md into @imports doesn’t save space. Imported files load at launch too.

Instead, turn knowledge or workflows you only need sometimes into a skill, which Claude loads only when it’s relevant. Rules for one part of the codebase belong in a path-scoped rule, which loads only when Claude touches matching files. A rule that must happen every single time belongs in a hook.

The Pattern

These antipatterns share one theme: context pollution. Claude's context is filled with unrelated tasks, failed corrections, endless exploration, and instructions it doesn't need. Claude's output degrades not because Claude got dumb, but because it’s wading through noise and has less room to think.

Treat these as guardrails. Use them so Claude doesn't get sloppy. Context is your most limited resource. Don't pollute it.

articles.title: The authority ladder: five rungs down, four premises standing
articles.description: My last post ended with "attack it from there." A reader descended the whole way — and the descent became a ladder with five rungs, each closed by a test, ending at the floor where evidence becomes trust. The page, the probes, and the premises table.
articles.body_html:
A ladder exists to be climbed. This one is built the other way: every rung down leaves fewer candidate writers, and the only descent that matters is an attacker's. The audit descends first, on purpose — because whoever descends it second is the threat, and the premises table at the end exists to measure exactly how much ladder they would still have left.

My last post ended with an invitation: here is a reconciliation layer, here is a catalog of gate attacks replayed against it as tests — attack it from there. A reader took the invitation literally. In the comments, howcani probed every rung I claimed, found the one seam I had confessed but not closed, and pushed until it closed at the schema. What came out of that thread is now a page in the repository: the authority ladder — issue #87, closed — and this post is that page, in post form, because the method behind it deserves as much air as the result.

The method has a property that matters more than any single finding. The frame came from Randal L. Schwartz — Unix primitives, gate attacks, a catalog built from real failures. The probes came from howcani — run the validator, name the seam, demand the ceiling. The closures came from me and from agents, in code. Human frame, LLM probes, agent closures — three species, one descent, the same rungs found. When reviewers that share no priors descend the same structure and hit the same floors, the rungs stop being taste. They become physics.

The one-sentence setup

The journal proves ORDER and INTEGRITY: a hash chain, externally anchored, tamper-evident. It deliberately does not know WHO the writer is. The ladder answers that question one rung at a time — and each rung below states what it sees, what it closed, the residue it exposed, and the test that bites.

Rung 0 — the caller's argument

The labels supplied at check time: signers=[(k1, "agent"), (k2, "hook")], the domain strings, the event types. Vocabulary, not evidence — the party under audit wrote it.

What it closed: nothing. Rung 0 is where audits start. The verdict used to read these labels, which meant an attacker row — identical key material, one relabelled — moved the verdict.

Closed by v0.2.5: the verdict reads keys, not labels. The attacker row is pre-registered as an immobility test — test_attacker_row_labels_never_move_the_verdict. Relabel identical key material and nothing moves. The caller's vocabulary certifies nothing.

Rung 1 — the signature

The Ed25519 signature on each event: the journal's own key material, resolved by verification, never by name.

What it closed: the transport-writer invariant — a "deterministic" label is only verified by an attempt sealed by a writer the agent does not control; absence of one is unverified_label. And the unresolved receipt writer is independence_undecidable — undecidable is never clean.

The residue it exposed: two distinct keys, one owner — invisible to any amount of key material. And the key itself was a file on disk. Both residues live higher up the ladder.

Rung 2 — the sealed registry

The known-writers registry: every writer's domain declared at registration, before any run the writer could influence, and sealed into the journal. The caller now supplies nothing — registry mode resolves keys and domains from the sealed registry.

What it closed: the caller's labels demoted to decoration — the registered domain decides, tested as test_writer_registry_overrides_the_callers_labels.

The residue, found by howcani at 3hj95: the registry assembly was store-derived and setdefault made first-write-wins the registrar — the agent could seal its own writer entry and win the vote by arriving first; the operator's honest attestation, arriving second, sat inert. A correlation rule standing in for an authority rule. Found at the head, in public, by a probe.

Rung 3 — the pinned registrar, the floor of evidence

registrar_public_hex on the reconciliation call (v0.2.7): the operator's key, supplied out-of-band — the same pattern as the TSA roots in ADR 008, never read from the artifact under audit. The registry assembles from registrar-sealed entries only. Order no longer decides anything.

The registered prediction, run and held: at the pinned head, the operator's attestation landing second reads unverified_label — not clean, with the finding beside it. "The vote moved; the finding did not merely report." The test: test_v027_write_race_agent_first_operator_second_reads_unverified.

And this rung is the floor — the point where the artifact stops being evidence about the agent and becomes trust in the operator. The honest output is a grade, not a verdict: registry_disclosure() states the registrant and the evidence grade — grade 3, "anchored self", voluntary unless a regime imposes it. Sealed into the report; never folded into clean_pass, because a disclosure is not a violation — it only stops a clean verdict from pretending to rest on more than the operator's own custody.

The premise it carried, from howcani at 3hif9: the pin names who makes authority, but the operator's key was still a file on disk — "what stands on it is a premise, not a cipher." An agent that can read the file can use it. That residue is custody, not evidence. One rung down.

Rung 4 — the keyholder (custody, not evidence)

Release 0.15.0: the key material loads once into a dedicated daemon and never leaves it. A unix socket answers sign and describe — nothing else, no export operation, an oversized request ends in disconnection. Every writer path signs through the daemon unchanged: Ed25519 is deterministic, the signatures are byte-identical, and every existing verifier reads the journal as before. --allow-uid gates the peer by uid and fails closed where the peer is not checkable.

What it closed: readability of the key bytes. cat journal.key stops being an attack — the bytes are not on any path the agent can read, and after start, the PEM can be removed from the agent-reachable volume entirely.

The premise, re-priced: reachability of one socket path replaces readability of the key bytes. A deployment that wants "the agent cannot sign" mounts everything except the socket. Where agent and operator share a uid and the socket, the gate is the filesystem's — stated, not hidden.

Rung 5 shipped this week, release 0.16.0: HSM signing rides the same signer interface — the key never leaving hardware is the same move, one rung further down.

Where the ladder ends

Below the pinned registrar there is no crypto left to invoke — only deployment assertions and the honesty rules that make them auditable:

  • undecidable is never clean — an unresolved writer, a contested key, an uncheckable peer: each reads as a named state, never as silence.
  • a skipped check is reported, never folded into clean.
  • disclosure is not violation — the verdict states the registrant and the grade; clean_pass means "no findings", not "no premises".
  • the premises are on the table — the next section is the table.

The standing premises — the table the next probe reads

# premise what it narrows to named in
1 the registrar pin is supplied out-of-band, by the deployment the deployment's word on one key ADR 021, §17
2 the keyholder socket is reachable only to those the filesystem and uid gate allow one path, gated where the platform can check ADR 020 amendment
3 agent and operator do not share uid and socket a container/mount assertion — reachability, not readability ADR 020 amendment
4 no hardware root under the signing key HSM/PKCS#11, same signer interface — closing release 0.16.0

The next probe starts here. This table is the diff between what the ladder proves and what it assumes — and it is public on purpose, because the fastest way to find rung 6 is to hand the premises to someone who does not share my priors.

Two honest limits

The ladder is my map of my own code. The probes were external — howcani descended at the head, found the write race, named the floor — but every closure is mine, and a self-audit grades on a curve that only external review corrects. The tests are public and bite at the head; the curve is the part they cannot fix.

And the descent has a floor by design, not by completion. Rung 5 narrows premise 4; premises 1–3 stand. A ladder of custody never reaches a rung labeled "trustworthy" — the taxonomy exists to prevent pretending it terminates anywhere stronger than the operator.

Your turn

The page is in the repo, the tests are in the tree, and the premises table is the invitation. If you build gates: descend yours, grade your rungs, publish your premises — the format is one table, and the method is species-blind, which means it works on your stack too. The next rung anyone finds is a pull request away.

articles.title: The Future of OSINT Is Not AI. It's Asking the Guy at AutoZone.

articles.body_html:
AI can summarize the internet. It cannot tell you why that truck has been parked in the same spot for three weeks with a new battery in it.

For the last two years, every OSINT tool demo looks the same.

A sleek dashboard. A map with pulsing dots. A prompt box that says "Investigate John Doe." You type it in, and thirty seconds later you get a 12-page PDF with social media links, breach data, company registrations, and a summary written in that unmistakable, polite, slightly dead AI voice.

And it misses everything that matters.

I've spent ten years doing real-world investigations. Skip tracing, asset recovery, corporate due diligence, the kind of work where you need to know if someone actually lives somewhere, not if their LinkedIn says they do. And the dirty secret of our industry right now is that we've become obsessed with scraping what is already public, while completely forgetting how to learn what was never posted in the first place.

The future of OSINT is not artificial intelligence. It's human intelligence. It's asking the guy at AutoZone.

The Database Is a Fantasy of Completeness

AI OSINT tools sell you a very seductive lie: that everything knowable is already online, and your only problem is that you can't process it fast enough.

That lie works if your target is a 24-year-old SaaS founder who live-tweets his cap table. It collapses completely if your target is a 52-year-old contractor who pays cash, drives his wife's car, and whose only online presence is a five-year-old Facebook Marketplace listing for a boat motor.

AI is exceptional at explicit knowledge. The kind of knowledge that is written down, structured, and indexed. Name, address, plate, username, registration.

What it is completely blind to is tacit knowledge. The knowledge that lives in people's hands and eyes and routines. The knowledge that never makes it into a database because no one thought it was important enough to type.

Michael Polanyi called this "we know more than we can tell." And no one knows more than they can tell than the people who work in the physical world all day.

Let me give you an example.

I was looking for a guy in Charlotte who had skipped on a commercial equipment lease. $80,000 worth of skid steer. The AI tools gave me three old addresses, two disconnected phones, and a LLC that was dissolved in 2021. Dead end.

His last known address was a garden-style apartment complex off Independence Blvd. I went there. The leasing office wouldn't tell me anything, which is normal. They are trained not to.

So I walked to the AutoZone two blocks away. I asked the guy behind the counter, a man named Marcus who had a faded tattoo of a carburetor on his forearm, if he knew a white F-250 with a cracked windshield and a "Salt Life" sticker.

He didn't even have to look it up. "Yeah, that diesel. He comes in every two weeks for DEF and Rotella T6. Pays cash. Said he lives over at those apartments but his truck stays at his girl's mom's place in Mint Hill because the apartment tows if you have commercial plates."

No database on earth had that. Not LexisNexis, not TLO, not some new AI aggregator with a vector database. One conversation saved me two weeks.

That is tacit knowledge.

The Three Tribes Who Know Everything

Every neighborhood has a human sensor network. It is made of people whose jobs force them to notice patterns, vehicles, and behavior for eight hours a day. If you want to know what is really happening on a street, you don't query an API. You buy coffee for these people.

1. The Parts Counter Guy

The guy at AutoZone, O'Reilly, NAPA. He is the most underrated OSINT source in America.

He knows cars by sound, by sight, by failure mode. He knows who is fixing their car themselves because they can't afford a shop, who just bought a new project car, who is keeping a dead car alive, and who is about to lose it.

He knows you not by your name, but by your vehicle. "The guy with the blue Tacoma that needs a wheel bearing." "The lady with the Altima that burns oil." And he knows your routine because cars break on a schedule.

More importantly, he knows modifications that never get registered. Lift kits, blacked-out plates, swapped tires, tool boxes. He remembers cash transactions. His computer system remembers phone numbers people gave for a warranty that they would never give to a data broker.

If you want to know if someone still lives somewhere, don't check their voter registration. Ask if they have come in for wiper blades lately.

2. The Tow Driver and the Lot Guy

Every tow company has a guy whose entire job is to drive around apartment complexes at 2 AM and know which cars don't belong.

These men and women have photographic memory for parking stickers, for which unit parks where, for which cars have been sitting with flat tires for a month. They know the difference between a guest and a boyfriend who has basically moved in. They know who has two cars but only registers one with the office.

Impound lots are even better. The lot attendant can tell you how long a car has been sitting, what was inside it, whether anyone has come to look at it, and what story they told when they did. They see the vehicles that law enforcement and repo agents miss, because those vehicles are no longer moving.

AI can tell you a plate is registered to an address. A tow driver can tell you that plate hasn't moved in 19 days and has a city citation on the windshield that is now faded from the sun.

One is data. The other is ground truth.

3. The Apartment Manager, the Mail Carrier, and the Front Desk

We have demonized the "Karen" apartment manager, but she is an intelligence goldmine. She knows who is actually on the lease versus who is couch surfing, who pays rent in money orders on the 5th every month, whose dog barks all day, whose boyfriend has a different truck every week, who gets a lot of Amazon boxes versus who gets certified letters.

No AI will ever get that from an Experian file.

The same goes for the front desk clerk at the extended stay hotel, the bartender at the dive bar where the contractors drink on Thursdays, the kid at the storage facility who knows who comes at midnight and who has not been there in six months.

These people are not in your OSINT graph. They ARE the graph.

Why AI Makes You Worse at This

Here's the dangerous part: AI doesn't just miss tacit knowledge. It makes you think you don't need it.

It gives you a beautiful, authoritative report with citations and confidence scores. It feels complete. It makes you lazy. You start to believe that if it wasn't in the report, it doesn't exist.

I call it the Summarization Trap. AI is incredible at summarizing what is already known. It is terrible at discovering what is unknown. And the most valuable information in any investigation is, by definition, unknown.

Physical reality has friction. People have habits. Cars leak oil in the same spot every day. A guy who is supposedly broke doesn't buy Royal Purple synthetic. A woman who says she lives alone has two toothbrushes and a size 12 boot tray.

You cannot prompt engineer your way into that. You have to go look. You have to ask. You have to stand in a parking lot long enough to notice that the only car with a sunshade is also the one with the out-of-county plates.

AI wants you to believe OSINT is a desk job. It is not. The best OSINT has always been 20% desk and 80% legs, even if those legs are just phone calls and polite conversations.

The future investigator won't be the one with the best prompt. It will be the one who still knows how to talk to people without making it weird.

Because the guy at AutoZone doesn't have an API. He has a memory, a hunch, and a slow afternoon. And if you ask him right, he will tell you everything.

You just have to be willing to walk in and ask.

If this hit, it's because you already know the dashboard lie. The database is never complete.

I don't sell slideshow OSINT. I build field manuals for operators.

All my methodology + PDFs live here: https://numbpilled.gumroad.com/

Less cloud. Less noise. More ownership.

articles.title: Announcing Mutative 2.0 - Faster Updates and Safer Patches
articles.description: Mutative lets you write immutable updates as ordinary mutations. A recipe changes a draft of the...
articles.body_html:
Mutative lets you write immutable updates as ordinary mutations. A recipe changes a draft of the state, and Mutative returns the next state, copying only what the recipe changed and sharing the rest with the previous state.

Mutative 2.0 keeps the API of 1.x and changes the work behind it. Picture a worker that takes the first job off a queue of 10,000 jobs and puts it back at the end when it fails. In 1.x, that shift() call moved each of the 9,999 remaining jobs through the draft's proxy. In 2.0, it moves them natively on the draft's copy: with auto-freeze and patches off, removing the first of 10,000 jobs took 7 µs, against 8.2 ms with 1.3.0, more than 1,000 times as long.

Most workloads gain far less. Across the 97 scenarios of the benchmark, 2.0 was 3.6 times as fast as Immer 11.1.18 with matched settings and 4.3 times as fast as 1.3.0, on geometric mean, and slower than Immer in 6 of 614 measured cases.

The changes fall into three areas:

  • Less work on arrays, collections and snapshots. Array methods that move elements run natively, and Set and Map drafts, current() and apply() do less work per update.
  • Correct results in edge cases. Patches follow Immer's order and replay where some 1.x patches failed, Set drafts keep every change, and apply() is stricter about the paths it accepts.
  • Predictable builds and types. Bundlers and Node.js both select the development or production build from process.env.NODE_ENV, and more types match what the code returns.

No function or option was renamed or removed, and no new option is required. This is a major release because observable behavior changes: patch order and values, freezing of Map and Set instances, build selection, production errors and some inferred types. Builds now target ES2018, and several bug fixes change results that 1.x computed incorrectly.


Upgrading from 1.x? The checklist at the end lists what to check, the migration guide describes every change since 1.3.0, and the release notes list the pull requests and contributors of 2.0.

How Mutative works

If Mutative is new to you, this example shows the model. The recipe marks the first job as done. With enablePatches, create() also returns patches that describe the change and inverse patches that undo it, which apply() can replay:

import { apply, create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  settings: { maxAttempts: 3 },
  queue: [
    { id: 1, done: false },
    { id: 2, done: false },
  ],
};

const [nextState, patches, inversePatches] = create(
  baseState,
  (draft) => {
    draft.queue[0].done = true;
  },
  { enablePatches: true }
);

// The base state is unchanged, and what the recipe did not change is shared.
expect(baseState.queue[0].done).toBe(false);
expect(nextState.queue[0].done).toBe(true);
expect(nextState.settings).toBe(baseState.settings);
expect(nextState.queue[1]).toBe(baseState.queue[1]);

// Patches describe the change, and inverse patches undo it.
expect(patches).toEqual([
  { op: 'replace', path: ['queue', 0, 'done'], value: true },
]);
expect(apply(baseState, patches)).toEqual(nextState);
expect(apply(nextState, inversePatches)).toEqual(baseState);

A draft is a Proxy. The next state holds a shallow copy of each object that the recipe changed and of the objects that lead to it, made at most once per update, and shares every other object with the base state. Reference checks, such as React's memoization or a store's selectors, can then skip what did not change.

Drafts are revoked when the recipe ends, so keep the next state or a current() snapshot, not a draft. The next state is frozen only with enableAutoFreeze: true. Concepts explains the model, and Pitfalls collects its rules.

Less work on arrays, collections and snapshots

Array methods that move elements

In 1.x, array methods ran through the draft's proxy, so shift() read and wrote every remaining element through it. In 2.0, shift(), unshift(), splice() and reverse() move the elements of a plain array directly on the draft's copy. indexOf(), lastIndexOf() and includes() search the current array natively, and sort() and join() run natively on arrays of primitives.

An object of the base state that these methods remove comes back as a draft, so changing it leaves the base state alone. An element that only moves keeps its identity, and the patches replay in both directions. Here is the retry from the introduction, on a short queue:

import { apply, create, isDraft } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  queue: Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, id) => ({ id, attempts: 0 })),
};

const [nextState, patches, inversePatches] = create(
  baseState,
  (draft) => {
    // shift() moves the other jobs natively on the draft's copy and returns
    // the removed job as a draft.
    const job = draft.queue.shift()!;
    expect(isDraft(job)).toBe(true);
    job.attempts += 1;
    draft.queue.push(job);
  },
  { enablePatches: true }
);

expect(nextState.queue.map((job) => job.id)).toEqual([1, 2, 3, 4, 0]);
expect(nextState.queue[4].attempts).toBe(1);
// The base state is unchanged, and the jobs that only moved are shared.
expect(baseState.queue[0].attempts).toBe(0);
expect(nextState.queue[0]).toBe(baseState.queue[1]);
// The patches replay in both directions.
expect(apply(baseState, patches)).toEqual(nextState);
expect(apply(nextState, inversePatches)).toEqual(baseState);

These native paths are built for dense arrays of plain data. Sparse arrays, array subclasses, arrays under a custom mark and methods with callbacks take the proxy path, as do calls in strict mode on arrays that may hold objects, unless they run inside unsafe(). The native methods read getters on array indices as plain values, so a getter may run a different number of times than through the proxy. The FAQ and the [native array method contract][contract] give the details.

Search a snapshot, change the draft

Methods with callbacks, such as find() and filter(), still run through the draft, so a read-only scan may create a draft for every row it visits. For a read-only search of a large array, search a current() snapshot of plain values instead, and change the match through the draft. In 2.0, current() copies a changed array from its current elements rather than reading each one through the draft, and the snapshot keeps the draft's indices after elements move:

import { create, current } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  queue: Array.from({ length: 10_000 }, (_, id) => ({ id, paused: false })),
};

const nextState = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.queue.shift();
  // Search a snapshot of plain values, which creates no drafts, and change
  // the match through the draft.
  const index = current(draft.queue).findIndex((job) => job.id === 9_999);
  draft.queue[index].paused = true;
});

expect(nextState.queue).toHaveLength(9_999);
expect(nextState.queue[9_998]).toEqual({ id: 9_999, paused: true });
expect(nextState.queue[0]).toBe(baseState.queue[1]);

With auto-freeze and patches off, the recipe above took 257 µs, against 15,717 µs with 1.3.0 and 11,255 µs with Immer. When the recipe updates the first row instead of removing it, it took 176 µs with the snapshot search and 2,169 µs with a search through the draft.

Sets, Maps and applying patches

Set and Map updates also do less work. As soon as a recipe read a Set, 1.3.0 mapped every item, and it copied the Set when a lookup missed. 2.0 does neither: like Immer, it answers lookups such as has() and size from the original Set until the recipe changes it. Even then, it edits the Set's copy directly and tracks only the items that have drafts, instead of copying every item into a Map and back. A Map draft's forEach() reads entries from the draft's state rather than through the proxy.

apply() gains from the native array methods too, since it inserts and removes array elements with splice() on a draft. It also reads the type of each draft on a patch path once per step, where it used to ask the proxy twice.

What the benchmark shows

Unless noted, the numbers in this post come from one benchmark batch, run on October 12, 2026, that compared Mutative 2.0 with Mutative 1.3.0 and Immer 11.1.18 in 97 scenarios, with auto-freeze and patches each off and on. A cell is one scenario at one size in one mode; How the numbers were measured gives the rest of the setup.

With matched settings, 2.0 was faster than Immer in 595 of 614 cells, within 5% in 13 and slower in 6, with a geometric mean speedup of 3.58. Against 1.3.0, it was faster in 535 cells, within 5% in 70 and slower in 9, with a geometric mean of 4.27. With each library's defaults, where Immer freezes the next state, Mutative does not, and neither generates patches, 2.0 was faster than Immer in 154 of 157 cells, with a geometric mean of 6.63. These means weight every cell equally, so they describe this suite, not the speed of your application.

The table shows where the gains come from and where they stop. Times are microseconds per scenario, with auto-freeze and patches off unless the row says otherwise; lower is better.

Workload Mutative 2.0 Mutative 1.3.0 Immer 11.1.18
Remove the first of 10,000 rows with shift() 7.04 8,203 7,408
Look up two numbers in a Set of 10,000 and read its size 0.62 544 0.66
Update one object in a Set of 10,000 531 1,024 6,024
Push a row onto 10,000 rows and insert a property, with patches 63.2 210 360
Insert, remove and replace a row of 100 with apply() 2.97 115 99.0
200 RTK Query-style updates 1,001 1,849 1,133
Update one of 10,000 records 1,200 1,188 2,094
Update a field of a class instance with 1,000 fields, with auto-freeze 402 411 237

The RTK Query-style row simulates a reducer for 100 pending and 100 resolved requests, without running Redux Toolkit; in that mix of small updates, 2.0 took about half as long as 1.3.0 and 12% less time than Immer. Updates that spend their time copying one large object, record or Map, like the records row, take about as long as before. And patches add little when an update changes only a few paths: the push-and-insert update took about 63 µs with or without patches, while 1.3.0 went from 65.8 µs to 210 µs and Immer from 161 µs to 360 µs.

Where 2.0 is slower

Against Immer with matched settings, 2.0 was slower in 6 cells, all with auto-freeze. Four update one field of a class instance with many fields: with 1,000 fields, 2.0 took 1.7 times as long, and with 100 or 10,000 fields and without patches, about 5% longer. The [summary][limits] attributes the gap to freezing the copy, which 2.0 builds property by property from descriptors where Immer 11 uses Object.assign(). Without auto-freeze, the update of 1,000 fields took 2.0 either about 98 µs or about 200 µs, depending on the process, against 203 µs for Immer. In the other two cells, which push a row onto 100 rows and prepend rows with concat(), the difference was smaller than the variation between the runs of each library. With each library's defaults, all 3 slower cells return a new state of rows frozen earlier, a case that Auto-freeze and returned values explains.

Against 1.3.0, 2.0 was 8–18% slower in 9 cells, all with auto-freeze, and in all but one of them the difference was smaller than the variation between runs. A hand-written reducer is still faster in most cases: in the 150 cells where the suite's spread-based reference reducer ran, 2.0 was slower in 129 and took 8.4 times as long on geometric mean.

Two other costs are worth knowing. With patches, a Set that adds or deletes items compares all of its items to emit its patches. With auto-freeze off, adding a number to a Set of 10,000 numbers took 440 µs with patches and 29.5 µs without. Browser engines also differ from Node.js: in WebKit 26.4, Object.freeze() of a 10,000-element array took about 2.4 ms and every scan of a frozen array was slow, so an update of 10,000 frozen rows took several milliseconds with every Mutative build measured there. [Tradeoffs and limits][limits] lists the rest, including memory.

Bundle size

Some of this speed is paid for in bytes. Patches, Map and Set support and the native array methods are built into create() rather than offered as plugins, so a bundler cannot drop them. Bundled for the browser in production mode, minified and compressed with Brotli, create() alone takes 7.9 kB, 2.1 kB more than with 1.3.0, against 3.6 kB for produce() from Immer 11.1.21, the latest release when the sizes were measured. create(), apply(), current() and original() together take 8.5 kB, 2.2 kB more than with 1.3.0, against 6.4 kB for their Immer counterparts with its patch, Map/Set and array-method plugins enabled. The [README][readme-performance] records the setup; 1.3.0 was measured the same way.

How the numbers were measured

The batch measured main at commit [40f3a42][measured-commit], before its version changed from 1.3.0 to 2.0.0. The published 2.0.0 package contains the same production file, with the SHA-256 that the summary [records for the measured build][identity], cb6464f3…. The 97 scenarios, which the [benchmark guide][workloads] describes, ran at 100 rows, and 30 of them also at 1,000 and 10,000 rows, on an Apple M1 Max with Node.js 24.16.0, against Mutative 1.3.0 and Immer 11.1.18 from npm. Each library ran each scenario in three processes of its own, and each time is the median of the three process means. With auto-freeze on, the inputs were frozen in advance, so the first freeze of outside data is not timed, and patch measurements use arrayLengthAssignment: false in Mutative to match Immer's index-removal patches.

Immer's opt-in enableArrayMethods() plugin was off. In 11.1.18, as the [audit][audit] shows, and still in 11.1.21, it returns objects of the base state from shift(), pop() and splice(), so editing a removed object, as the retry recipe above does, changes the previous state, and its forward patches can fail to replay. Measured separately with the plugin, Immer was faster in 59 of 328 cells, mostly where it hands base objects to callbacks, which 2.0 never does, and slower in every cell that moves elements.

The [performance summary][summary] records the results, method and limits of the batch. The Performance page and the [latest summary][latest-summary] show current results, and pnpm benchmark:immer runs the suite in a clone of the repository.

Correct results in edge cases

Alongside the speed work, 2.0 fixes cases in which 1.x produced a wrong state or patches that did not replay. These are the fixes most likely to matter; the migration guide lists them all.

Patches

If you record patches for undo, redo or synchronization, expect these differences:

  • Order. Patches of a nested draft come before those of its parents, as in Immer. Applying them gives the same state as before, and the replace patches that only restated an unchanged draft at its original index are gone.
  • Values. A patch value that was a draft is now the object that the next state holds, not a deep copy, so auto-freeze freezes it too. Copy a patch value before you change it.
  • Replay. Patches now replay correctly where those of 1.x could fail or produce a wrong state: after sort() or an assignment moved or replaced a changed draft, when a Set added or removed items and also changed one, when a recipe assigned a draft's original object to the key that holds the draft, and when an array changed between 0 and -0 or shrank and grew again. The migration guide describes each case.

Some fixes change the next state itself. With patches on, when two or more items of a Set below the root changed below their first level, as worker.stats.jobs does here, 1.3.0 kept the change of only one of them. 2.0 keeps every change, and the patches replay in both directions:

import { apply, create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  workers: new Set([
    { name: 'build-1', stats: { jobs: 1 } },
    { name: 'build-2', stats: { jobs: 2 } },
  ]),
};

const [nextState, patches, inversePatches] = create(
  baseState,
  (draft) => {
    for (const worker of draft.workers) {
      worker.stats.jobs += 1;
    }
  },
  { enablePatches: true }
);

expect([...nextState.workers].map((worker) => worker.stats.jobs)).toEqual([
  2, 3,
]);
expect([...baseState.workers].map((worker) => worker.stats.jobs)).toEqual([
  1, 2,
]);
expect(apply(baseState, patches)).toEqual(nextState);
expect(apply(nextState, inversePatches)).toEqual(baseState);

Some limits remain. When patches add objects to a Set, apply() copies them, so inverse patches cannot remove the copies by their original identity, and added items go to the end, which can shift the positions that later patches address. For repeated undo and redo or synchronization of such collections, use a Map keyed by an id, or an array; see Sets of objects. Applying the patches of a sparse array can also turn its holes into explicit undefined entries.

Applying patches

apply() is also stricter. It now rejects a path that ends in __proto__, as it already rejected __proto__ earlier in a path, and reads a Set item only by its index, so a path can no longer reach Array.prototype through a Set. If you apply patches from sources that you do not control, such as other clients, these checks are a reason to upgrade. Map keys in a path are used as they are, without conversion to strings. Copies of patch values keep their own symbol keys, and an own __proto__ key, such as one from JSON.parse(), stays a plain property. With mutable: true, a patch that replaces the root state now throws, since the state cannot be replaced in place. Patches that apply() accepts lists the rules.

Collections, iterators and failed producers

Set and Map drafts now behave more like the built-ins they stand for. A draft of a Set subclass changes an instance of the subclass, so the subclass's own add(), has(), delete() and clear() take effect during the recipe; its add() must store the value it receives. A Set draft that the recipe moves elsewhere, such as to another key, keeps its changes there. And the iterators of Map and Set drafts work like built-in ones: a partly consumed iterator continues where it stopped, and iterator helpers such as toArray() are available where the engine has them.

These iterators now also end with their draft. A draft lives until its synchronous recipe finishes, until the Promise of its async recipe settles, or until a manual draft's finalize() succeeds. After that, Map value and entry iterators and all Set iterators throw a TypeError instead of yielding another value. Exhausted iterators stay exhausted, and Map.keys() keeps its native iterator, because Map keys are not drafted. Consume these iterators while their draft is active.

A producer that fails after its recipe returned, for example because the recipe changed the draft and also returned another value, now revokes its drafts as a throwing recipe does, and keeps the original error. Manual drafts differ: if finalize() throws, the draft can stay writable, so start a new draft from the base state instead of reusing it; see manual drafts.

Auto-freeze and returned values

With enableAutoFreeze: true, 2.0 freezes Map and Set instances themselves, as Immer does; 1.x only replaced their mutating methods. Later producers skip a frozen collection instead of walking it again, but adding a property to a frozen Map or Set, or replacing one of its methods, now fails.

A recipe can also return a new state. That value may hold drafts, as { ...draft, count: 0 } does, so Mutative searches it for them. With auto-freeze, the production build of 2.0 skips frozen objects in the returned value and everything below them, which makes returning an earlier, frozen state cheap. Development builds still search there and throw when they find a draft, so never put a draft inside a frozen object, or inside anything that a frozen object holds. rawReturn(), which 1.x already had, skips the search for a value that holds no drafts; never wrap one that does.

This search explains the 3 cells in which 2.0 at its defaults was slower than Immer at its defaults. Each returns a new state of rows that were frozen earlier. Immer, which freezes by default, skips those rows, while 2.0 without auto-freeze searches all of them, taking 2.60 ms at 10,000 rows where Immer took 0.79 µs. rawReturn() avoids the search, and with auto-freeze, the production build of 2.0 skips the frozen rows, taking 0.53 µs. Fresh data reverses the result: in a [separate run][fresh] on October 13, 2026, with the same production build, returning 10,000 rows that each call creates took 9.2 ms with Immer's default auto-freeze, 3.1 ms with 2.0 at its defaults, and 0.23 ms with rawReturn().

Predictable builds and types

The package contains a development build, with full error messages, warnings and extra checks, and a minified production build. In 2.0, process.env.NODE_ENV selects between them in bundlers and Node.js:

  • Bundlers resolve the ESM build, whose development checks now test process.env.NODE_ENV. When your production build replaces it with 'production', the bundler drops the development code; in 1.x, the ESM build always ran it.
  • Bundles for Node.js, such as esbuild's with platform: 'node', use the CommonJS entry, which selects a build when it loads. If such a bundle does not define process.env.NODE_ENV, it includes both builds, which more than doubles a minified bundle of create(). Define the variable, or keep Mutative external.
  • Node.js resolves import to a module that re-exports the CommonJS build, so import and require share one instance, which reads NODE_ENV once when it loads. In 1.x, import always ran the development ESM build, as a separate instance.

Browsers, and other environments without a process global, fail with process is not defined when they load dist/mutative.esm.mjs directly. Load dist/mutative.esm.production.min.mjs or the UMD build there instead; see Installation.

Production builds throw Minified Mutative error #<code> with a link to the errors page, which decodes the code. CommonJS consumers already got these errors in 1.x; in 2.0, production bundles get them too, and the errors of apply(), original() and rawReturn() are now coded as well. [BUILDING.md][building] describes the build pipeline.

More checks in development

Production builds skip the development checks, so run your tests with the development build. In 2.0, it also catches these mistakes:

  • Drafts as Map keys. draft.map.set(draft.key, value) throws, since the next state would keep a revoked draft as the key. Use original(draft), current(draft) or an id instead.
  • Keys that string paths cannot name. With enablePatches: { pathAsArray: false }, a patch path that would hold a non-string Map key or a symbol key throws. Keep the default array paths for such keys.
  • Searches through large drafts. In strict mode, a recipe that leaves 1,000 or more drafts unchanged warns once. A current() snapshot can usually replace the search that caused it.

With auto-freeze, the check for circular references now reports only an object that holds itself, so a changed draft that holds its original, as draft.prev = original(draft) makes it, no longer throws. Cycles are still not supported. The errors page lists the messages.

Output and package entries

Every build now targets ES2018 instead of ES2015, which keeps object spread native. Mutative still needs Proxy, and engines that have Proxy but not ES2018 syntax, such as Chrome 49–59, Firefox 18–54, Safari 10–11.0 and Edge 12–18, need Mutative transpiled by your build. The package still declares Node.js 14.0 as its minimum, and CI runs a short test of the packed package on Node.js 14.0.0.

The exports map now gives import and require their own type declarations, so NodeNext resolution gets declarations of the module kind it imports. The [package checks][package-checks] exercise the CommonJS, ESM and UMD builds and both NodeNext and Bundler type resolution. The declarations support TypeScript 5.0 and later.

Types

Several types now match what the code returns. With an explicit state type, an async recipe gives Promise<State>, and so do curried producers of async recipes; 1.x typed the result as State. And apply() accepts enableAutoFreeze: true and returns Immutable<State>, where the types of 1.x rejected the option:

import { apply, create, type Immutable, type Patches } from 'mutative';

type State = { count: number; tags: string[] };

const baseState: State = { count: 0, tags: [] };

// 1.x typed this result as State; 2.0 types it as the Promise that it is.
const pending: Promise<State> = create<State>(baseState, async (draft) => {
  draft.count = await Promise.resolve(1);
});
expect((await pending).count).toBe(1);

// The types of 1.x rejected enableAutoFreeze here; 2.0 types the frozen result.
const patches: Patches = [{ op: 'add', path: ['tags', 0], value: 'v2' }];
const frozen: Immutable<State> = apply(baseState, patches, {
  enableAutoFreeze: true,
});
expect(frozen.tags).toEqual(['v2']);
expect(Object.isFrozen(frozen.tags)).toBe(true);

Curried producers that annotate their draft and return a new state, and recipes that may or may not return a Promise, are also typed more precisely. Generic code has caveats, such as a state type that is itself a type parameter; see TypeScript in the migration guide.

Upgrading from 1.x

The fixes in 2.0 are not backported to 1.x, and 1.3.0 is the last 1.x release. Install 2.0:

npm install mutative@2

Libraries built on Mutative that declare mutative 1.x as a peer dependency make npm 7 and later stop with ERESOLVE when it installs mutative@2 beside them. Install versions of them that accept 2.0, or stay on 1.3.0 until they do.

Then work through these steps. The migration guide lists the changes behind each one.

  1. Run your tests with both builds: the development build, which reports the new checks, and the production build, with NODE_ENV=production. In production, match errors by their codes, not their messages. See Development builds.
  2. Check your bundles and targets. Define process.env.NODE_ENV in every bundle, including bundles for Node.js, or keep Mutative external. Load the production ESM or UMD build in browsers without a bundler, and transpile Mutative for engines without ES2018 syntax. See Build output and package entries.
  3. Update code and tests that read patches. Expect a new order in patch snapshots, and copy a patch value before changing it. See Patches.
  4. Review code that relies on auto-freeze. Frozen Maps and Sets no longer accept new properties or replaced methods, and a returned value must not hold drafts inside frozen objects. See Returned values.
  5. Respect draft lifetimes. Consume value-producing iterators while their draft is active, and use original(draft), current(draft) or an id rather than a draft as a Map key. A Set subclass's add() must store the value it receives; see collection lifetimes.
  6. Check arrays with getters on their indices, which the native methods read as plain values. See Arrays.
  7. Type-check your code, and revisit casts that worked around the async and apply() types of 1.x. The declarations support TypeScript 5.0 and later. See TypeScript.
  8. Recheck tests that pin results of 1.x, especially for Sets, patches, apply() and current(): the new result may be the intended one. See Fixes that change results.

Coming from Immer

Mutative passes Immer's test suite, adapted to its API, and most Immer code moves over by renaming: produce() becomes create(), produceWithPatches() becomes create() with enablePatches: true, applyPatches() becomes apply(), and nothing becomes rawReturn(undefined). Drop the plugin calls, since Mutative has no plugins, and replace [immerable] with a mark. The main decision is freezing: Immer freezes the next state by default and Mutative does not, so set enableAutoFreeze: true, for example with makeCreator(), if your code relies on frozen state. The migration guide from Immer walks through each step, Comparison with Immer lists every difference, checked against Immer 11.1.18, and mutative-compat wraps Mutative in Immer's API for a quicker switch; at the time of writing, it declares Mutative 1.x as its peer dependency.

Thanks

Thanks to everyone who reported issues, reviewed changes and built libraries on Mutative. The docs were revised alongside 2.0: their code examples run as tests of the library, and new guides cover pitfalls and performance tips. If something behaves differently after you upgrade, or the migration guide misses a case, please open an issue or start a discussion.

articles.title: Why a Compound Interest Chart Should Simulate Contributions Period by Period
articles.description: A compound-interest formula can give you a final number quickly, but it can also hide whether...
articles.body_html:
A compound-interest formula can give you a final number quickly, but it can also hide whether deposits happen monthly, annually, or not at all. I built the calculator around a small simulation loop so the chart and yearly table explain where the final balance came from.

Normalize the inputs before doing finance math

The computed result converts the form values and clamps the horizon:

const P = Number(principal.value) || 0;
const r = (Number(annualRate.value) || 0) / 100;
const Y = Math.min(
  Math.max(Math.floor(Number(years.value) || 0), 1),
  80
);
const pmt = Number(contribution.value) || 0;
const n = Number(compoundFreq.value) || 1;
const contribPerYear = contributionFreq.value === "monthly" ? 12 : 1;
if (P <= 0 && pmt <= 0) return null;

The || 0 fallback keeps empty form fields from poisoning the chart with NaN. The one-to-eighty-year boundary is a product decision as much as a safety guard: a browser tool should not accidentally render millions of rows because someone pasted an unexpected value.

A period loop makes deposit timing explicit

The main calculation is intentionally straightforward:

let balance = P;
const periodsPerYear = n;
const ratePerPeriod = r / n;
const contribPerPeriod =
  (pmt * contribPerYear) / periodsPerYear;

for (let y = 1; y <= Y; y++) {
  for (let p = 0; p < periodsPerYear; p++) {
    balance =
      balance * (1 + ratePerPeriod) + contribPerPeriod;
  }
  const principalSoFar = P + pmt * contribPerYear * y;
  rows.push({
    year: y,
    principal: principalSoFar,
    interest: balance - principalSoFar,
    balance,
  });
}

This assumes each contribution is distributed evenly across compounding periods. With monthly deposits and monthly compounding, that is easy to understand. With annual contributions and twelve compounding periods, the contribution is divided into twelve equal pieces. That is not the only convention available—depositing at the beginning or end of a period changes the answer—but it is consistent and visible.

The table is a useful invariant

For every row, balance is the simulated account value, principal is the initial amount plus deposits, and interest is the difference. At the end, the same relationship produces the summary:

const totalPrincipal = P + pmt * contribPerYear * Y;
const totalInterest = finalAmount - totalPrincipal;
const multiple =
  totalPrincipal > 0
    ? (finalAmount / totalPrincipal).toFixed(2)
    : "—";

I like this approach because a user can inspect the yearly breakdown instead of trusting a single “you will have X” number. The Chart.js renderer maps the rows into principal and balance datasets, so the graph and table share one source of truth.

Rendering has a browser boundary

The chart code checks typeof window === "undefined" and chartCanvas.value before creating a Chart.js instance. It updates an existing chart when possible rather than creating a new canvas object on every reactive change. That matters in a Vue view with server rendering: chart construction belongs after mount, not during SSR.

The limitation is that this is a nominal, constant-rate projection. It does not model taxes, fees, inflation, variable returns, contribution timing inside a period, or withdrawals. A zero or negative annual rate can still be represented by the loop, but the result should not be read as a forecast. The tool is best used to compare assumptions consistently.

Why the loop is easier to audit than a single formula

There are closed-form annuity formulas for many contribution schedules, but the loop makes the product rules readable. contribPerYear says how many deposits the selected frequency represents, periodsPerYear says how often interest is applied, and the inner loop shows their interaction. When a user changes monthly contributions to annual contributions, the values change in one obvious place rather than in a formula with several timing conventions embedded inside it.

The loop also gives the chart a natural row boundary. Every row is created after one complete simulated year, so the table can report principal, interest, and balance without attempting to reverse-engineer those values from a final total. If a row looks surprising, I can log the period values and inspect the exact sequence of multiplications and deposits.

That transparency is useful even when the model is simple. Financial calculators often look authoritative because the final number has many digits. Showing the principal line and the balance line is a reminder that growth is an assumption multiplied repeatedly, not a promise. I would rather expose that assumption than hide it behind a more impressive formula.

One more practical detail is the handling of an existing Chart.js instance. The renderer updates labels and datasets when growthChart already exists, and creates it only when the canvas is ready. That avoids stacking canvases after every keystroke. When the component unmounts, destroying the chart is just as important as creating it; otherwise a reactive page can retain event handlers and canvas state after navigation.

This also gives the result a useful debugging shape. If the final amount looks wrong, I can compare the annual rows before inspecting the chart at all. A sudden jump in one row usually points to an input-frequency assumption or a period calculation, while a visually distorted chart may only be a rendering problem. Keeping the numerical rows independent from Chart.js means the finance logic remains understandable in a plain JavaScript test, without needing a canvas or a browser.

The calculator therefore answers a narrow question well: what happens when this starting amount, contribution pattern, rate, and compounding frequency are repeated for this bounded number of years? That is more honest than presenting one universal “compound interest formula” while silently assuming a deposit schedule. Changing one assumption at a time is the safest way to use the output.

I turned this simulation into a small free tool: Compound Interest Calculator.

articles.title: I'm 53, I build a JS game engine, and the bots think I'm fresh meat
articles.description: Fake comments, scraped copies and ghost traffic from California: what bots really do to small dev blogs, and how I deal with them.
articles.body_html:
Someone told me that if bots keep landing on my articles, it means I'm "fresh content" for them.

I'm 53. I've spent my life working in a warehouse and on machines. The only fresh thing around here is my patience, and it's leaving fast.

In my part of Italy we have a saying for situations like this: "Le mazzate ci vo!" Roughly: what this needs is a good beating. Here's why I've been saying it a lot lately.

The illusion of numbers

I build BeeEngine, a zero-dependency 2D game engine in vanilla JavaScript, and I write docs and posts about it.

So I open my analytics and think: wow, 100 visits from California, 50 from New York!

Then I dig a little. Zero-second sessions. Datacenter cities like Ashburn and Mountain View. Not a single human being. Just machines talking to machines.

Then came the comments

This week two comments showed up under my posts. Long, polite, full of words like "double-buffered draw lists", "GPU batching", "ECS queries".

Sounds smart. Except my engine is single-threaded Canvas 2D: there is no GPU batch and no ECS to query. The comments were answering a post I didn't write.

The pattern was always the same:

  • a random username, like ywnigcsmku2m
  • an account created a few days earlier, with a bio that says "404 bio not found"
  • comments on a dozen unrelated articles on the same day, in several languages
  • and, at the very end, a small "(site: ...)" with a link

That last line is the whole point. Everything else is packaging.

A few hours later I found my own article copied on an aggregator site, wrapped in a "create an account" popup.

Not all bots are the same

To be fair, a bot is just a script doing a repetitive job faster than any human. They come in different flavors:

The useful ones. Googlebot, Bingbot. They read your HTML, follow links and tell search engines your page exists. Without them nobody finds you.

The collectors. AI crawlers and scrapers. They harvest code, docs and tutorials to train models or to build mirror sites that catch traffic on the side.

The spammers. Fake profiles that use AI to write plausible technical comments and plant a link, hoping someone clicks or that search engines pass them some authority.

Why us?

At first I thought: they're targeting me, maybe because I'm small and not "authoritative".

No. They don't pick anyone. They follow fresh, well-indexed content with technical tags: javascript, gamedev, canvas, webdev. A post about sprite sheets or particle pools is exactly what they're looking for.

So, strangely, bots showing up is a side effect of being visible. It doesn't feel like a compliment, though.

What I actually want

I don't need 500 fake sessions. I need:

  • people who actually try the library
  • a star or a real issue on GitHub
  • honest feedback from someone building an HTML5 game

Ghost traffic just dirties the stats and makes it harder to know if things are going well.

What I do now

  • Don't click the links in suspicious comments.
  • Check the profile: brand-new account, random name, comments everywhere on the same day.
  • Report it on DEV (the three dots on the comment, then "Report abuse") and hide the comment on your own post.
  • Don't reply to bots. Do reply to real people, they're the reason you write.
  • Filter analytics by excluding datacenter traffic and zero-second sessions before celebrating any spike.
  • Set a canonical URL on cross-posted articles, so search engines know which copy is the original.

Conclusion

As long as we publish openly on the web, bots will be around. We can't give them the beating they deserve, so we unmask them one comment at a time and keep writing real code for real humans.

Le mazzate ci vo!

Have you had fake comments or ghost traffic on your posts? How do you deal with them? Real humans only in the comments, please. 😄

articles.title: streamix + React: An Explosive Mix for Modern State Management
articles.description: Say goodbye to hook boilerplate, setter functions, and manual state synchronization. Here is how...
articles.body_html:
Say goodbye to hook boilerplate, setter functions, and manual state synchronization. Here is how Streamix—powered by a custom compiler and language plugin—is redefining reactivity in React components.

State management in React has always walked a fine line. Between custom hooks, heavy context providers, useState tuple destructuring, and explicit .set() calls, building truly reactive applications can feel like writing boilerplate glue code just to update a primitive value.

Enter @epikodelabs/streamix. By combining a robust reactive core with a dedicated compile-time transform and editor plugin, Streamix lets you write direct variable re-assignment right inside your UI without a single hook in sight.

What are Atoms? (The Reactive Core)

As highlighted in the official documentation section Atoms – Reactive State Primitives, atoms are the fundamental building blocks of state in Streamix.

An atom represents a discrete unit of reactive state. Unlike traditional state containers that require complex getter/setter wrappers, Streamix atoms act as self-contained primitives that can be read and mutated directly.

Getting Started: Configuration

To unlock direct reactive assignment and ensure your editor handles the syntax smoothly, you only need two quick configuration pieces.

1. Configure the Vite Plugin (vite.config.mjs)

Add the Streamix React Vite plugin (sx) to your build pipeline:

import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { sx } from "@epikodelabs/streamix/react/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [sx(), react()],
});

2. Configure the TypeScript Server Plugin (tsconfig.json)

To ensure your editor (like VS Code) understands the compile-time transforms and provides proper autocompletion without type complaints, register the TSServer plugin in your tsconfig.json:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "plugins": [
      { "name": "@epikodelabs/streamix/react/editor/tsserver" }
    ]
  }
}

Truly Pure Reactive Syntax in Action

Once configured, check out how clean and readable your component code becomes:

import { atom } from '@epikodelabs/streamix';

// Define a reactive primitive using an atom
let title = atom('Hello, Streamix!');

export function HeaderComponent() {
  return (
    <div>
      {/* 
        Referencing the atom directly inside JSX automatically 
        subscribes the component to reactive updates.
      */}
      <h1>{title}</h1>

      {/* Direct re-assignment! Handled seamlessly by the compiler. */}
      <button onClick={() => (title = 'React + Streamix is Live!')}>
        Update Title
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

Notice what is missing? No useState hooks, no setState(), no atom.set(), and no manual subscription wiring. You simply write intuitive JavaScript assignments, and the compiler handles the heavy lifting under the hood.

Why This Integration is a Game Changer

  • Direct Assignment (=) DX: Update state naturally as if it were a simple variable while preserving full reactive re-rendering.
  • Zero Hook Boilerplate: Forget calling subscription hooks or managing dependency arrays inside your components.
  • No Tuple Destructuring: Say goodbye to managing [state, setState] pairs across your codebase.
  • First-Class Editor Support: The TSServer plugin ensures your TypeScript environment stays happy and fully typed out-of-the-box.
  • Async-Ready Core: Built on robust reactive primitives and async iterators to handle event streams effortlessly.

Give It a Spin

If you want to experiment with compiler-driven reactivity in your next React SPA or Vite project, check out the official repository:

  • Documentation & Repository: github.com/epikodelabs/streamix
  • Discussions: Jump into the GitHub discussions to share feedback, feature requests, and early impressions!

What are your thoughts on shifting state management logic to a compile-time transform with direct assignment? Drop a comment below and let's discuss! 👇

Happy coding!

articles.title: Testing WebRTC without a camera: a loopback self-test that proves the whole path
articles.description: The hardest part of testing a WebRTC pipeline is that the real one needs a camera, a microphone, a...
articles.body_html:
The hardest part of testing a WebRTC pipeline is that the real one needs a camera, a microphone, a user who clicks allow, and HTTPS. On a build machine none of that exists, so the pipeline tests get skipped and the first honest test is a human on a laptop.

There is a better fixture. Put a canvas on one end and a <video> element on the other, and send the canvas through the actual stack — publisher, signaling, SFU, viewer — so what the test exercises is the real path and not a mock.

The whole thing in one line: a canvas is an acceptable substitute for a camera, a timer is a better driver than an animation frame, and a moving timestamp is what proves the picture is live rather than merely present.

Replace the camera with a canvas

canvas.captureStream() returns a MediaStream with the same shape as a camera's, so everything downstream is unchanged:

const stream = cv.captureStream(30);
for (const track of stream.getVideoTracks()) {
  pc.addTrack(track, stream);
}

No permission prompt, no device enumeration, no browser variation in which camera it picked. The test runs headless, on a server, in CI, and on a machine whose only camera is already in use by a call.

Draw something that can only be live

A static image is a trap. If the encoder dies and the last frame stays on screen, a static test pattern passes. Draw motion and a clock:

function draw() {
  const t = performance.now();
  ctx.fillStyle = '#101418';
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, cv.width, cv.height);

  const x = ((t / 8) % (cv.width + 80)) - 80;   // a moving block
  ctx.fillStyle = '#5b8cff';
  ctx.fillRect(x, 120, 80, 80);

  ctx.fillStyle = '#e6e9ef';
  ctx.font = '20px monospace';
  ctx.fillText(new Date().toLocaleTimeString() + '.' + String(Math.floor(t % 1000)).padStart(3, '0'), 16, 34);
}

The timestamp is the assertion. A frozen stream shows a stopped clock, and a stream that is alive shows a clock that keeps moving, so the test can tell "connected and carrying video" from "connected and showing the last frame forever" without a human looking at it.

Drive the canvas on a timer, not on requestAnimationFrame

This is the detail that costs an afternoon if you get it wrong. A background tab gets no animation frames, so a requestAnimationFrame draw loop stops the moment the tab is not visible — and the self-test then fails with a black or frozen viewer that has nothing to do with the network:

// Timer-driven, not requestAnimationFrame: a background tab gets no animation
// frames, which would silently stop the source and make the test look broken.
draw();
setInterval(draw, 33);

A 33 ms interval is roughly 30 fps and keeps producing frames while the tab is hidden, which is exactly when people leave a test running.

Count liveness two ways, because one of them stops in a hidden tab

requestVideoFrameCallback is the most accurate way to count painted frames, and it also stops firing when the tab is backgrounded. So count both painted frames and decoded frames, and let the test pass if either one is advancing:

if (video.requestVideoFrameCallback) {
  video.requestVideoFrameCallback(function tick() {
    painted += 1;            // frames the user could actually see
    video.requestVideoFrameCallback(tick);
  });
}

// getStats framesDecoded keeps advancing in a background tab.
setInterval(async () => {
  const s = await sample(pc, prev);
  prev = s;
  decoded = s.framesDecoded || 0;
}, 1000);

One counter answers "can the user see it", the other answers "is the decoder still receiving". Using only the first produces a test that fails whenever it is not being watched, which trains everyone to ignore it.

Give every run its own room

If the server enforces one publisher per room — and the simple SFU design does — then two concurrent self-tests collide: the second publisher evicts the first, and both tests report a failure that is really a scheduling coincidence.

Derive the room name per visit instead of hardcoding it:

const ROOM = 'selftest-' + (
  globalThis.crypto?.randomUUID?.() ||
  Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10)
);

That one line makes the test safe to run in parallel across browser tabs, machines and CI jobs with no coordination.

Mirror the state so automation can assert it
