A test whose only output is pixels cannot be automated. Publish the state on a global object and assert on numbers:

const st = {
  publisher: 'connecting',
  viewer: 'connecting',
  frames: 0,      // frames painted, via requestVideoFrameCallback
  decoded: 0,     // frames decoded, via getStats - works in a background tab
  w: 0,
  h: 0,
  kbps: null,
  ice: '',
};
window.__st = st;

Now the assertion is boring and reliable: wait for ice to be connected, wait for decoded to exceed a threshold, and confirm the resolution is what you asked for. A driver script can do that in a few lines, and a failure tells you which of the three did not happen.

What this test does and does not prove

It proves the path end to end: track creation, offer/answer through the server, the SFU's fan-out, decoding, and the resolution and bitrate the session settled on. It catches the majority of regressions, because most of them break the path rather than a corner of it.

It does not prove TURN works from outside your network — that needs a host with a different NAT, which is why the relay probe is a separate test. It does not prove camera or microphone behaviour, because there is no camera. And it does not prove quality under loss; for that you need a network emulator, not a loopback.

Those boundaries are worth stating in the test itself. A self-test that claims to cover everything gets trusted for everything and then quietly lies.

The fixture, in order

  1. Source from a canvas, not a camera — headless, no permissions, no HTTPS requirement.
  2. Draw a moving element and a monotonic timestamp so a frozen frame cannot pass.
  3. Drive the canvas with a timer, because a hidden tab stops animation frames.
  4. Count painted frames and decoded frames, and accept either as liveness.
  5. Give each run a unique room so parallel tests cannot evict each other.
  6. Expose the state on a global so assertions are numeric, not visual.
  7. Be explicit about what the test does not cover, and keep the relay and loss tests separate.

This loopback test ships with the self-hosted WebRTC kit — canvas publisher, server relay, viewer, and the same stats panel the production viewer uses — so the whole path can be verified before a camera or a network is involved:

https://lowlatencykit.com/

The free relay probe, which covers the one thing the loopback test cannot, needs no account:

https://lowlatencykit.com/test/turn/

articles.title: One camera, many viewers: the fan-out details that decide whether viewer #2 works
articles.description: The first viewer is easy. You put a TrackLocalStaticRTP on the server, you write the publisher's...
articles.body_html:
The first viewer is easy. You put a TrackLocalStaticRTP on the server, you write the publisher's packets into it, and the tile lights up. Then a second viewer joins and you find out that "forward the RTP" was never a complete design.

The single-viewer case hides five decisions. Each one is small, and each one is the difference between a demo and a session that behaves the same way for viewer number two.

The whole thing in one line: the publisher sends one stream, the server's egress scales with viewers, and every viewer needs its own negotiation plus its own keyframe request.

The publisher's uplink does not grow, and that is the entire point

In a mesh, three viewers means the publisher encodes and uploads three streams. In an SFU it uploads one. The server reads each incoming packet once and writes it to a local track that is bound to every viewer's sender:

local, err := webrtc.NewTrackLocalStaticRTP(codec.RTPCodecCapability, remote.ID(), remote.StreamID())
if err != nil {
    return
}

// One reader for the upstream, one local track, N senders bound to it.
go func() {
    for {
        pkt, _, readErr := remote.ReadRTP()
        if readErr != nil {
            break
        }
        if writeErr := local.WriteRTP(pkt); writeErr != nil {
            break
        }
    }
}()

The consequence people miss is where the bandwidth lands. The field technician on a phone keeps a single modest uplink no matter how many people are watching, and the server pays the multiplication. That is the right trade for a support call — the person on site has the worst connection in the system, and the server has the best one.

It is also the number you have to watch when you plan capacity: egress, not ingress, and it grows linearly with viewers per session.

The new viewer's black tile is a keyframe problem

The first viewer connects while the encoder is producing frames, so a keyframe arrives quickly. A viewer that joins ten minutes into a session receives inter-frames that reference a keyframe it never saw. RTP flows, framesReceived climbs, and the tile is black until the publisher's encoder happens to emit the next keyframe — which, for a long GOP, can be many seconds.

The fix is to relay the viewer's feedback upstream. Browsers already send a Picture Loss Indication when they cannot decode; the server's job is to carry it to the publisher. But a PLI carries the SSRC it is about, and a PLI that arrives from a viewer is about the server's local track, not the publisher's upstream track:

ssrc := uint32(t.remote.SSRC())
for _, p := range pkts {
    switch pkt := p.(type) {
    case *rtcp.PictureLossIndication:
        pkt.MediaSSRC = ssrc
    case *rtcp.FullIntraRequest:
        pkt.MediaSSRC = ssrc
    case *rtcp.TransportLayerNack:
        pkt.MediaSSRC = ssrc
    }
}
if err := t.pubPC.WriteRTCP(pkts); err != nil {
    return
}

Forward the packet unchanged and the publisher sees feedback about an SSRC it does not own, ignores it, and the new viewer waits out the GOP. Rewrite MediaSSRC to the publisher's value and the keyframe arrives in milliseconds. This one line is the difference between "the second viewer is broken" and "the second viewer is instant", and nothing in the browser tells you which one you are looking at.

Negotiate all the tracks in one offer, not one offer per track

A publisher's ontrack fires once per track. Audio and video often arrive within milliseconds of each other, and a naive implementation answers each one immediately, which puts two setLocalDescription cycles in flight for the same viewer. That is offer glare on your own connection, and the symptoms are intermittent in the way that wastes an afternoon.

Batch them. A short timer that coalesces whatever arrived into a single offer per viewer is enough:

func (r *Room) scheduleNegotiateLocked() {
    if r.negTimer != nil {
        return
    }
    r.negTimer = time.AfterFunc(250*time.Millisecond, func() {
        r.mu.Lock()
        defer r.mu.Unlock()
        r.negTimer = nil
        for v := range r.viewers {
            r.negotiateViewerLocked(v)
        }
    })
}

Two details make it safe: the timer is stored per room so a burst of track arrivals collapses into one callback, and the callback re-takes the lock and re-checks the state, because 250 milliseconds is plenty of time for a viewer to leave.

RTCP reads need a real buffer

The control channel looks trivial until it does not. Read it with a buffer sized for the largest datagram you can receive, not for the packet you expect:

buf := make([]byte, 1500)
for {
    n, _, err := sender.Read(buf)
    if err != nil {
        return
    }
    pkts, err := rtcp.Unmarshal(buf[:n])
    if err != nil {
        continue
    }
    // ...
}

An undersized buffer turns into a short read, Unmarshal fails, and the feedback is silently dropped — which surfaces as poor quality that only appears on networks sending large compound RTCP packets.

When the publisher changes, every viewer is stale

If the publisher disconnects or republishes, the viewers' PeerConnections are holding transceivers that belong to a session that no longer exists. Patching them is not worth it; tear them down so the next negotiation starts clean:

// resetViewersLocked tears down every viewer's PeerConnection so the next
// negotiation starts from scratch. Caller must hold r.mu.

This pairs with the client-side ladder: the viewer's full-rejoin fallback exists precisely because the server rebuilt its side, and a viewer that reuses its old connection negotiates successfully and receives nothing.

The honest limits of this design

Being explicit about the edges is more useful than pretending they are not there:

  • One publisher per room. Multiple publishers and stream mixing are a different product; this fan-out assumes a single source that everyone watches.
  • The codec is forwarded as-is. The server does not transcode, so if the publisher switches codec mid-session, viewer connections have to be rebuilt.
  • No simulcast or SVC in this version. Every viewer receives the same encoding, which is right for a support call with a handful of viewers and wrong for a 500-person webinar.

Knowing which of those you need is most of the architecture decision. For one technician showing a fault to two or three people, the simple version is not a compromise.

The six things that make viewer #2 work

  1. Read the upstream once; bind the same local track to every viewer's sender.
  2. Budget server egress, not publisher uplink, for capacity.
  3. Relay viewer PLI/NACK upstream with the publisher's SSRC so a late joiner gets a keyframe immediately.
  4. Batch track arrivals into one offer per viewer instead of one offer per track.
  5. Give RTCP reads a full-size buffer and handle unmarshal failures explicitly.
  6. Rebuild viewer connections when the publisher's session ends, and let the client escalate to a full rejoin.

I built this fan-out, the batched negotiation, the RTCP relay and the client-side recovery ladder into a self-hosted WebRTC kit in Go — signaling server, SFU and browser clients in one binary, with a diagnostics panel that shows the selected candidate path and per-leg stats:

https://lowlatencykit.com/

The field-assist guide, which is the deployment this design is tuned for, is here:

https://lowlatencykit.com/guides/remote-field-assist-mobile-webrtc/

articles.title: The six getStats numbers that actually tell you what broke
articles.description: getStats() returns a few hundred fields across dozens of records, and almost all of them are useless...
articles.body_html:
getStats() returns a few hundred fields across dozens of records, and almost all of them are useless for diagnosis. The problem is not that the data is missing. It is that the numbers which matter only mean something in combination, and a dashboard that prints all of them tells you nothing.

These are the six worth putting on a screen, in the order I would look at them.

The whole thing in one line: the selected candidate pair tells you the path, the inbound counters tell you whether media arrived, and the outbound reason tells you why the encoder is holding back.

1. The selected candidate pair, and the candidate types behind it

This is the one everyone gets wrong, because getStats() reports many candidate-pair records and only one of them is the path your media is actually on. Print the wrong pair and you will confidently announce a direct connection while the session is relayed, or the reverse:

stats.forEach((r) => {
  if (r.type === 'local-candidate' || r.type === 'remote-candidate') cands[r.id] = r;
  if (r.type === 'candidate-pair' && (r.selected || r.state === 'succeeded') && r.currentRoundTripTime != null) {
    pair = r;
  }
});

Note the extra condition. Requiring currentRoundTripTime != null filters out pair records that exist but never carried a round trip — which is most of them on a NAT-heavy session. Without it, a "succeeded" pair with no measured RTT can win and you report a path that was never used.

The types are not on the pair. They live in separate records that the pair refers to by id, so you have to join them:

const l = cands[pair.localCandidateId];
const rm = cands[pair.remoteCandidateId];
out.localType = l ? l.candidateType : null;   // host | srflx | prflx | relay
out.remoteType = rm ? rm.candidateType : null;

host → host means a direct path on the same network. relay → relay means both sides are going through TURN, which is the expected state behind a carrier NAT and the first thing to verify when someone says the relay is broken. Skipping the join is why people conclude "it is always relayed" or "it is never relayed".

2. Inbound bitrate, which requires two samples

bytesReceived is a cumulative counter. You cannot read a rate out of a single snapshot, which is why so many quick debugging scripts print a number that keeps growing and call it bitrate:

// Pass the previous sample in; the delta is the rate.
if (prev && prev.bytes != null && r.bytesReceived != null && now > prev.t) {
  out.bitrateKbps = Math.round(((r.bytesReceived - prev.bytes) * 8) / (now - prev.t));
}
out.bytes = r.bytesReceived;

One unit trap lives in that line: (bytes delta * 8) / milliseconds is kilobits per second only because the division by a duration in milliseconds yields bits per millisecond — which is bits per second divided by a thousand. Get the units wrong here and your numbers are off by 1000, which looks like a codec problem.

3. framesPerSecond and resolution

These tell you whether the stream is alive at the quality you asked for. A stream that negotiated 1280×720 and settles at 320×180 is not broken; it is being told to back off, and the next two numbers say by what.

Read frameWidth/frameHeight from the inbound video record rather than from the video element's videoWidth. The element reports the decoded frame, which lags behind a change and is zero until the first frame decodes — the exact moment you most need a number.

4. qualityLimitationReason on the outbound side

This is the single most underused field in WebRTC diagnostics. When the encoder reduces resolution or frame rate, it says why:

if (r.type === 'outbound-rtp' && r.kind === 'video') {
  out.qlr = r.qualityLimitationReason || null;   // bandwidth | cpu | other | none
  ...
}

bandwidth means the estimator decided the path cannot carry more, and the fix is the network or the bitrate ceiling. cpu means the sender could not encode fast enough, and the fix is on the machine — resolution, hardware encoding, or too many tabs doing the same thing. other is usually a screen-share capture path that cannot keep up. Those are three different investigations, and without this field you are guessing between them.

5. framesDecoded versus framesReceived

This pair is how you separate transport from decode. Packets arriving while decoded frames stay flat means the media reached you and could not be turned into pictures — codec parameters, a missing keyframe, or a hardware decoder that gave up.

out.freezeCount = r.freezeCount != null ? r.freezeCount : null;
out.framesDecoded = r.framesDecoded != null ? r.framesDecoded : null;

freezeCount is the browser's own opinion that the picture stopped, which is a useful cross-check on your own frame-gap detection. If your 2-second frame-gap timer says "frozen" and freezeCount is still rising while framesDecoded is not, you are looking at decode, not at the network. If framesDecoded is climbing and the user still reports a frozen tile, the problem is downstream of the decoder — rendering, the element, or the application.

6. Jitter and the jitter buffer

Jitter on its own is a poor number to alarm on, because a jitter buffer exists precisely to absorb it. The informative value is the average time a frame spent waiting in that buffer, which you compute from two counters:

if (r.jitterBufferDelay != null && r.jitterBufferEmittedCount) {
  out.jbufMs = Math.round((r.jitterBufferDelay / r.jitterBufferEmittedCount) * 1000);
}

That is total buffer delay divided by frames emitted, scaled to milliseconds: the average per-frame hold. A buffer sitting in the tens of milliseconds is doing its job. A buffer climbing into the hundreds means the network is delivering frames unevenly enough that latency is the price being paid to keep the picture smooth — and for a live support call, that trade is often the wrong one.

The table that fits on one screen

The rendering that is actually useful is thirteen rows and no graphs:

const rows = [
  ['Connection',     (s.connState || '-') + ' / ' + (s.iceState || '-')],
  ['Bitrate in',     s.bitrateKbps != null ? s.bitrateKbps + ' kbps' : '-'],
  ['Resolution',     s.w ? s.w + ' x ' + s.h : '-'],
  ['FPS in',         s.fps != null ? s.fps + ' fps' : '-'],
  ['Packets lost',   s.loss != null ? s.loss : '-'],
  ['Jitter',         s.jitterMs != null ? s.jitterMs + ' ms' : '-'],
  ['Jitter buffer',  s.jbufMs != null ? s.jbufMs + ' ms' : '-'],
  ['RTT',            s.rttMs != null ? s.rttMs + ' ms' : '-'],
  ['Path',           s.localType ? s.localType + ' -> ' + s.remoteType : '-'],
  ['Freezes',        s.freezeCount != null ? s.freezeCount : '-'],
  ['Bitrate out',    s.outKbps != null ? s.outKbps + ' kbps' : '-'],
  ['FPS out',        s.outFps != null ? s.outFps + ' fps' : '-'],
  ['Quality limit',  s.qlr != null ? s.qlr : '-'],
];

Sampled once a second, that table answers the questions support actually asks: is there a path, is media arriving, at what quality, and if it is degraded, is the encoder blaming the network or the CPU.

How to read it in one pass

  1. Path shows the candidate types. relay -> relay on a cellular session is correct, not a bug.
  2. Bitrate in and FPS in flat or zero with Connection connected is a media problem, not a signaling problem.
  3. Frames received climbing while Frames decoded stays flat means the media arrived and could not be decoded.
  4. Quality limit: bandwidth and Quality limit: cpu are different bugs with different owners.
  5. A jitter buffer in the hundreds of milliseconds is the latency you are paying for smoothness.
  6. Freezes rising is the browser agreeing with your own freeze detection.

I built this sampling and rendering into the diagnostics panel of a self-hosted WebRTC kit, next to the recovery ladder that acts on it — ICE restart first, full rejoin when that fails — so the numbers are visible while the failure is happening rather than reconstructed from a log afterwards:

https://lowlatencykit.com/

The guide that covers the network layers these numbers are measuring is here:

https://lowlatencykit.com/guides/remote-field-assist-mobile-webrtc/

articles.title: A frozen video tile and a working ICE state: the three-tier recovery ladder
articles.description: The support call starts the same way every time: "it says connected but the picture is stuck."...
articles.body_html:
The support call starts the same way every time: "it says connected but the picture is stuck." pc.iceConnectionState is connected. The signaling socket is open. Nothing in the logs is an error.

That is the failure this article is about, because the fix is not a config value. It is a recovery ladder: three tiers of escalating repair, each with a different cost, and a detection method that does not trust the connection state at all.

The whole thing in one line: connected describes the network path, not the picture, so a frozen tile and a healthy ICE state are entirely compatible.

Tier 0: detect on frames, never on ICE state

ICE state tells you whether a candidate pair was selected. It does not tell you whether frames are still arriving. A path that stops carrying media can sit in connected indefinitely, and a UI that renders a status dot from ICE state will happily show green over a black rectangle.

Ask the video element instead. requestVideoFrameCallback fires once per delivered frame, which makes it the cheapest possible liveness probe — no decoding, no stats parsing, and it is exactly the thing that stops happening when the picture freezes:

if (video.requestVideoFrameCallback) {
  video.requestVideoFrameCallback(function tick(now) {
    lastFrame = now;
    video.requestVideoFrameCallback(tick);
  });
}

setInterval(() => {
  const frozen = video.srcObject && performance.now() - lastFrame > 2000;
  // surface it; do not silently wait
}, 1000);

Two seconds is a deliberate choice: long enough that a normal keyframe interval or a momentary loss spike does not trip it, short enough that a user notices the recovery instead of giving up.

This is also the reason getStats() is a second opinion rather than the primary signal. It is the right tool for the cause — framesReceived climbing while framesDecoded stays flat means codec or keyframe, a climbing packetsLost means bandwidth — but polling it for liveness costs more and reports later than a frame callback.

Tier 1: an ICE restart, with a deadline

A restart is the cheapest repair, because it re-gathers candidates without tearing down the PeerConnection, the tracks, or the application state:

function tryRestart() {
  if (restarting) return;
  restarting = true;
  sig.send({ type: 'restart' });
  setTimeout(() => {
    restarting = false;
    if (pc && pc.iceConnectionState === 'failed') fullRejoin();
  }, 5000);
}

Two details in those nine lines are the whole lesson.

The restarting flag is what keeps a restart from stacking on top of itself while a previous attempt is still in flight. Without it, a 5-second timer that fires every second produces a restart storm, and the storm is worse than the original fault because now the server is doing new offers for a client that is still falling over.

The 5-second deadline is what stops the ladder from looping forever at tier 1. A restart fixes a path that changed — a phone that moved from Wi-Fi to cellular, a NAT mapping that expired, a route that shifted. It cannot fix a remote peer that is gone, and if you do not escalate, a client whose publisher has disappeared will retry restarts until the tab is closed.

Tier 2: the full rejoin, and why the old PeerConnection must die

When the server rebuilds its side — the publisher went away, or republished as a new session — the next offer is not a continuation of the session you were in. It is a new one. Reusing the old PeerConnection at that point produces the worst possible outcome: a connection that negotiates successfully, reports connected, and carries nothing, because the transceivers and the media state belong to a session the server has already discarded.

So the second tier is an explicit teardown, then a fresh socket:

function teardown() {
  if (pc) { pc.close(); pc = null; }
  video.srcObject = null;
}

function fullRejoin() {
  teardown();
  sig.reconnect();
}

Closing the PeerConnection is not cosmetic. It releases ICE agents and transceivers, and it makes the next createOffer a genuinely new negotiation instead of a delta against stale state.

The signaling layer needs two guards of its own

The ladder above is client-side recovery, but it depends on the socket underneath it behaving. Two guards matter, and both are absent from naive reconnect logic.

An epoch counter. A socket that closes after a newer socket has already connected would, without a guard, trigger a second reconnect and you end up with two live sockets and duplicated messages. Increment an epoch on every connect and let the handlers from stale sockets return early:

connect() {
  this.epoch += 1;
  const myEpoch = this.epoch;
  const ws = new WebSocket(this.url);
  ws.onclose = () => {
    if (myEpoch !== this.epoch) return;   // a newer socket already owns the state
    if (!this.closedByUser) this.retry();
  };
}

A send queue for the connecting window. The self-test path builds its offer during page load, before the socket has necessarily finished opening. A send() that returns false in that window silently drops the offer, and the symptom on the other side is "the server never answered" — a client bug that looks exactly like a server bug. Queue while readyState === CONNECTING and flush on open.

The retry itself is exponential with a ceiling, min(500 * 2^n, 8000), because a reconnecting client that hammers a server which is already struggling is a self-inflicted second outage.

What not to do

Do not keep the session alive with a client-side heartbeat timer. Hidden tabs throttle timers, and the tab is hidden precisely when a technician has put the phone in a pocket. Keepalives belong on the server, over the socket, for the reasons in the earlier article on reverse proxies.

Do not treat a restart as free and fire it on every hint of trouble. A restart re-gathers candidates and produces a new offer/answer; doing that on a loss spike turns a mild network blip into a visible glitch.

And do not hide the ladder from the user. A frozen tile with no indication is what makes someone close the tab. "Reconnecting" for two seconds, followed by a picture, is a product that looks like it is working.

The ladder, in order

  1. Detect on frames, not on iceConnectionState. A 2-second frame gap is a freeze.
  2. Try an ICE restart first, guarded by an in-flight flag.
  3. Give the restart a hard deadline. If it is still failed, escalate.
  4. Escalate to a full rejoin: close the PeerConnection, then reconnect fresh. A rebuilt server session needs a new negotiation.
  5. Guard the socket with an epoch counter and queue sends during CONNECTING.
  6. Back off exponentially to a ceiling, and keep keepalives on the server.

I built this ladder into the browser clients of a self-hosted WebRTC kit, together with the diagnostics panel that shows the selected candidate path, the freeze counter and the per-leg stats, so each tier can be watched failing and recovering on a real network instead of being taken on faith:

https://lowlatencykit.com/

The remote field-assist write-up, which walks the four network failure layers this ladder is designed to survive, is here:

https://lowlatencykit.com/guides/remote-field-assist-mobile-webrtc/

articles.title: Passkeys are a trap? I decoded two real ones to see what a website learns
articles.description: One of the most upvoted posts on Hacker News this weekend was an essay titled "Passkeys are a trap....
articles.body_html:
One of the most upvoted posts on Hacker News this weekend was an essay titled "Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them." Its argument is not that passkeys are weak. It concedes they can be far more secure than passwords and resist man-in-the-middle attacks. The worry is control: WebAuthn lets a website ask what kind of authenticator you used, and with attestation it can demand proof, which could one day lock out custom operating systems, unofficial passkey managers or anyone a site decides not to trust.

That is a policy argument, and it is worth having. But most of the people deciding whether passkeys become a trap are not standards bodies. They are developers writing a registration endpoint. So I generated two real passkeys and decoded exactly what they tell a website.

The setup

Chromium has a virtual authenticator you can drive over the DevTools protocol, so you can create real WebAuthn credentials in a headless browser without any hardware. I registered two:

  1. A synced passkey, the kind iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager creates, with the site asking for attestation: "none".
  2. A hardware security key, with the site asking for attestation: "direct".

Then I decoded each attestationObject with this script. It needs one dependency, cbor-x.

// Decode a WebAuthn attestationObject and print what the authenticator claimed.
// Usage: node flags.mjs <base64url attestationObject>
import { decode } from "cbor-x";

const att = decode(Buffer.from(process.argv[2], "base64url"));
const auth = att.authData;           // rpIdHash(32) | flags(1) | signCount(4) | ...
const f = auth[32];

const FLAGS = [
  [0x01, "UP", "user present (someone tapped or touched)"],
  [0x04, "UV", "user verified (biometric or PIN)"],
  [0x08, "BE", "backup eligible (can be synced to other devices)"],
  [0x10, "BS", "backed up (is currently synced)"],
  [0x40, "AT", "attested credential data included"],
  [0x80, "ED", "extension data included"],
];

console.log(`attestation format: ${att.fmt}`);
console.log(`attestation statement keys: [${Object.keys(att.attStmt).join(", ")}]`);
console.log(`flags byte: 0x${f.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")}`);
for (const [bit, name, meaning] of FLAGS) {
  console.log(`  ${f & bit ? "x" : " "} ${name}  ${meaning}`);
}
console.log(`  reserved bits 0x02 and 0x20: ${f & 0x22 ? "set" : "unset"}`);

What the synced passkey said 

attestation format: none
attestation statement keys: []
flags byte: 0x5d
  x UP  user present (someone tapped or touched)
  x UV  user verified (biometric or PIN)
  x BE  backup eligible (can be synced to other devices)
  x BS  backed up (is currently synced)
  x AT  attested credential data included
    ED  extension data included

What the security key said 

attestation format: packed
attestation statement keys: [alg, sig, x5c]
flags byte: 0x45
  x UP  user present (someone tapped or touched)
  x UV  user verified (biometric or PIN)
    BE  backup eligible (can be synced to other devices)
    BS  backed up (is currently synced)
  x AT  attested credential data included
    ED  extension data included

Three things stand out.

The flags are self-reported. With fmt: none the statement is empty. Nothing signs the claim that the user was verified or that the key is synced. The site simply takes the authenticator's word for it. That is the article's point: without attestation, software can say anything, and a site that wants certainty has to ask for attestation.

AT does not mean attested. This trips people up. The AT bit means the authenticator data contains the new credential's ID and public key. It is set on every registration, including the one with no attestation at all.

Attestation is a certificate chain. The security key returned x5c, an X.509 chain that identifies the authenticator's maker and, through its AAGUID, its model. A site can check it against the FIDO Metadata Service and refuse anything it does not recognise. That is the lever the article worries about.

Who actually pulls the lever

You do, in one line. Here is the default in SimpleWebAuthn, a widely used WebAuthn server library for Node:

import { generateRegistrationOptions } from "@simplewebauthn/server";

const options = await generateRegistrationOptions({
  rpName: "Acme",
  rpID: "acme.com",
  userName: user.email,
  attestationType: "none", // the default in v14; "direct" asks for the certificate chain
  authenticatorSelection: {
    residentKey: "preferred",
    userVerification: "preferred",
  },
});

The WebAuthn standard's own default for attestation conveyance is also none. Level 3 of the spec, which added the backup flags, became a W3C Recommendation on 25 August 2026. And even if you ask for attestation, Apple's synced passkeys do not provide it, according to passkey vendor Corbado. A consumer site that required attestation would lock out a large share of iPhone users on day one. So for consumer products today, the trap is mostly theoretical. Enterprises are the exception: requiring attested hardware keys for employees is a legitimate, common policy.

The rules I use for client apps

  1. Leave attestation at none for consumers. Only ask for it when a contract or regulator requires specific hardware.
  2. Never make passkeys the only way in. Keep a recovery path: a second passkey, TOTP or a verified email link. The article recommends TOTP and hardware keys, and supporting them costs you little.
  3. Accept any authenticator. Do not allowlist by AAGUID unless you have a reason you can write down. An allowlist quietly breaks every passkey manager you did not think of, and the user only finds out at the login screen. Bitwarden, 1Password, KeePassXC and the platform managers should all work.
  4. Read BE and BS, do not enforce them. They are useful for UX. If a user's only passkey has BS unset, it lives on one device, and losing that device means losing the account. Prompt them to add a backup or a second factor. Do not reject the credential.

Passkeys are the biggest phishing fix in a decade, and most of the control the article fears sits in the options object you write. Write it so your users can leave.

I set up authentication like this in every MVP we build at Axionry, and the rest of my default stack is in the SaaS MVP tech stack for 2026.

Sources: Passkeys are a trap (Non-Functional, 10 October 2026), Hacker News discussion, W3C Web Authentication Level 3, SimpleWebAuthn, Corbado on platforms without passkey attestation. articles.body_html:
At AnyPCBA, every board goes through a "health check" before it leaves the factory.

This isn't a single step—it's a chain of inspections: AOI, X-Ray, ICT, and FCT. Each one answers the same question: is this board safe to ship?

But many engineers have a fuzzy understanding of this chain. They know the factory "tests it," but not exactly what's tested, what can be caught, and what can't.

This article breaks down the inspection chain, layer by layer: what each test does, what it can catch, and what it can't.

Layer 1: AOI—Visible Defects Don't Stand a Chance

AOI (Automated Optical Inspection) is the first layer of the chain.

The principle is simple: high-resolution cameras capture the PCB surface and compare it against a "golden reference" image to find differences. It inspects visible solder joints and components.

What AOI can catch:

  • Missing or misaligned components: a component that wasn't placed, or placed incorrectly
  • Solder bridges: two pins that shouldn't be connected, connected by solder
  • Insufficient solder or cold joints: weak or insufficient solder joints
  • Tombstoning: a component standing on one end
  • Polarity errors: diodes, capacitors, or ICs placed in the wrong orientation

AOI is fast and high-coverage, well-suited for high-volume inspection. But its limitation is obvious: it can only see the surface.

For BGA and QFN packages, where the solder joints are hidden beneath the package body, AOI is helpless. The joints are under the chip—the camera can't see them.

Layer 2: X-Ray—Seeing Through the Joints
X-Ray inspection exists to solve AOI's blind spot.

X-Ray uses the penetrating power of X-rays to "see through" BGA bottoms, QFN bottoms, and through-hole interiors. It inspects solder joint quality hidden beneath packages.

What X-Ray can catch:

  • BGA voiding: bubbles inside solder balls, affecting mechanical strength and thermal conductivity
  • Solder ball bridging: adjacent balls under a BGA connected together
  • Missing or shifted solder balls: balls that should be there but aren't, or are misaligned
  • Poor via filling: incomplete fill inside vias, affecting reliability
  • QFN bottom joint defects: poor soldering on the thermal pad under the chip

X-Ray's limitation: it can see the "shape" of a solder joint, but it's hard to directly judge "strength" and "electrical performance." A joint that looks normal may actually be a cold joint.

Layer 3: ICT—Checking Electrical Connections

ICT (In-Circuit Test) uses probes to contact test points on the board and measure electrical parameters point by point.

It checks circuit connection integrity and component electrical performance.

What ICT can catch:

  • Opens: connections that should exist but don't
  • Shorts: connections that shouldn't exist but do
  • Component value deviation: actual resistance or capacitance outside spec
  • Component orientation errors: polarized components placed backwards
  • Missing components: components that should be installed but aren't

ICT's core metric is "coverage." Ideally, every electrical net should have a test point. But in reality, high-density boards have limited test point space, and coverage often falls short of 100%. Insufficient test point coverage means some defects may slip through.

Layer 4: FCT—Verifying Function

FCT (Functional Circuit Test) is the last layer—and the closest to "real-world use."

It powers up the board, simulates actual operating conditions, and verifies whether the board functions correctly.

What FCT can catch:

  • Functional abnormalities: a functional module that doesn't work
  • Performance below spec: excessive output noise, insufficient response speed
  • Timing issues: power-up sequencing or signal timing that doesn't meet requirements
  • Boundary condition failures: abnormal operation under extreme temperature or voltage

FCT's key lies in test case design. The more comprehensive the test cases, the more potential problems are caught. If test cases only cover "normal operating conditions," boundary condition issues will be missed.

One Chain, Different Roles, None Optional

Looking at all four inspections together, their roles are clear:


No single inspection is universal. AOI can't see BGA bottoms. X-Ray can't see electrical performance. ICT can't see functional behavior. FCT can't see long-term reliability.

That's why the chain must be complete. Each inspection covers the blind spot of the one before it.

What This Means for Hardware Engineers

1. Test coverage determines recall rate. If you only do AOI, BGA-related defects will slip through. If you only do ICT, functional abnormalities will slip through.

2. Test point design must happen at the design stage. ICT coverage depends on test point accessibility. If test points aren't reachable, even the best ICT equipment is useless.

3. FCT test cases must cover boundary conditions. Testing only "normal operating conditions" isn't enough. Temperature boundaries, voltage boundaries, and timing boundaries are all potential failure points.

4. Understand the boundaries of each inspection. Don't expect any single inspection to "handle everything." The value of the chain lies precisely in each inspection knowing what it can't see.

At AnyPCBA, our inspection chain covers AOI, X-Ray, ICT, and FCT, serving small-to-medium volume PCB and PCBA projects from 5 to 5000 pieces.

Specifically, what we can support includes:

  • Full AOI inspection: every board goes through automated optical inspection before shipment, checking component placement, solder joint quality, and polarity
  • X-Ray inspection: for BGA, QFN, and other hidden-joint packages, providing void rate, bridging, and offset detection
  • ICT testing: based on the customer's test point design, providing in-circuit test fixtures and test programs
  • FCT functional testing: working with customers to define test cases covering normal operating conditions and boundary conditions
  • Test point accessibility review: checking test point layout during DFM review, catching coverage gaps early
  • Test fixture design and fabrication: for small-to-medium volume projects, providing fast, low-cost test fixture solutions

Our manufacturing capabilities cover 2–64 layers, including HDI, rigid-flex, and high-frequency hybrid. We hold ISO 13485 (medical) and IATF 16949 (automotive) certifications. If you're working on a PCB or PCBA project that needs a complete inspection chain, contact us through our website.

What defects have slipped through inspection in your projects? Share your experience in the comments.
